# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]

## Department model and roles

- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Inferred (author uncertain — see Testing tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Rehab and return to play

- Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization — a support/advisory role, not a stated final-decision role. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (principle) / gap (no criteria stated)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Daily wellness-style subjective monitoring, dropped for general roster use, is explicitly kept in return-to-play scenarios specifically because subjective context still fills a gap objective testing can't. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- NordBord hamstring testing, dropped for roster-wide use, is explicitly retained for smaller, targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style). **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

*This is the thinnest discipline in the corpus — see Interview prep.*

## Injury risk and prevention

- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice.

## Recovery and sleep

- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
- Recovery appears in the department's own subcategory list of Athletic Performance (alongside strength, conditioning, speed, agility, power, nutrition, applied performance, sports psychology, RTP), but no specific recovery protocol, sleep target, or monitoring tool is described anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (named as a subcategory) / gap (no protocol stated)** [week1-lecture.md p.11]

## Nutrition and body composition

- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
- Body composition testing is capped at no more than 4 times per year. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- Anthropometrics (height, weight, muscle-to-fat ratio) are described as strongly associated with success in most sports and worth tracking even though they are owned by Performance Nutrition rather than Applied Performance. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- No nutrition decision rules, body-composition targets, or thresholds are attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; this appears to be a deliberate department-design choice (Performance Nutrition owns it) rather than an oversight.

## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach

- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.8]
- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
- Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost — elite athletes (cited examples: LeBron James, Deion Sanders) are described as outlasting and outperforming peers partly through tactical efficiency that lowers the physical output required to achieve the same result. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.8-9]
- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]

*Relatively thin as an independently-stated coaching philosophy in Eric's own voice specifically — most of this section is shared course/team material; see Interview prep.*

## Periodization and programming

- Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days — it can be extended to fit training themes around a real competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.17-18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
- In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21]
- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

## Data, technology and reporting

- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]
- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]
- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]

---

## No material found

None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.

---

## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- Books go through the ingest review gate (automated check plus an independent falsifying review) before atomization.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- Books go through the ingest review gate (automated check plus an independent falsifying review) before atomization.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

</system-reminder>

& "$env:USERPROFILE\bin\yt-dlp.exe" -f "best[ext=mp4]" -o "Lesson title.%(ext)s" "wistia:VIDEO_ID"

For an audio lesson, use `-f best`. A newly opened terminal may also recognize `yt-dlp` directly if your updated PATH has loaded.

1	# Podcast 1 — The False Promise of Technology without Discipline: summary
2	
3	Source: the locally generated transcript of the 9:58 audio. Timestamps refer to the downloaded media. The transcript is machine-generated and unverified; names and technical terms may be misrecognized. The Free Version audio is byte-identical (SHA-256) and has the same spoken content.
4	
5	The speaker, Jason Weber, argues that buying a technology and collecting its data do not automatically improve performance decisions. He defines *discipline* as the repeatable practices that make a tool useful. (00:00–02:19)
6	
7	- **Protocol drift:** A test may keep the same name while its warm-up, positioning, instructions, or acceptance rules change. Standardize and document these details before comparing results across sessions or staff. (02:19–03:03, 04:24–05:31)
8	- **Statistical interpretation:** Know the tool's and local process's reliability before calling an individual change meaningful. Distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action. (03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48)
9	- **Communication:** Dashboards alone do not assign decisions or keep departments aligned. Shared language, procedures, and recurring meetings help staff translate information into actions within the competition cycle. (03:17–03:38, 06:48–08:01)
10	
11	Weber places any single product within a wider performance system: measurements from one tool must be interpreted alongside other evidence and human judgment. He warns against treating a red dashboard indicator as an automatic reason to remove an athlete or collecting everything without a defined question. (03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19)
12	
13	His closing rules are to standardize data capture before scaling it, define what constitutes real change in the local environment, and judge the system by the decisions it supports. (09:19–09:51)
14

**00:04:30–00:04:34** We need to be able to do that in order to make sure that when we're making a call,

**00:04:34–00:04:39** when we're making a decision, when there's data driving into a dashboard that we've got 100%

**00:04:39–00:04:45** reliability on. And it needs to be documented. Reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in

**00:04:45–00:04:51** your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier. Because if that procedure

**00:04:51–00:04:55** changes just a little bit, the test becomes different. And we need to make sure we avoid

**00:04:55–00:05:02** that. So making sure your warm ups, familiarization, instructions, trials, all those things are locked

**00:05:02–00:05:07** in place. And they realistically should be part of your onboarding. So you get a new staff member

**00:05:07–00:05:13** in, this is how we operate. So I'll start with another concept. If you started a job this week

**00:05:13–00:05:18** as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to

**00:05:18–00:05:23** operate on New Year? This is where we're at. Now you might bully that one as strongly as I

**00:05:23–00:05:29** just put it, but you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow. Remembering

**00:05:29–00:05:35** that, when we talked about in the webinar, the world of SEAL team leader, Jocko Wilnick,

**00:05:35–00:05:42** discipline equals freedom. If we've got no discipline, when chaos happened, chaos does happen,

**00:05:42–00:05:48** then the questions start to come. And you don't get time. Discipline is going to equal reliability.

**00:05:48–00:05:54** Reliability equals confidence. Confidence means decisions you can defend when you need to. So

**00:05:54–00:05:59** again, if you're starting a job this week, don't sweat about buying new tech,

**00:05:59–00:06:03** order the tech you already have, and then earn the right to trust it. Good luck.

# Buchheit and Hader 2025 — Four-quadrant model for load and response monitoring

> **Citation**
> Buchheit M, Hader K. Data everywhere, insight nowhere: a practical quadrant-based model for monitoring training load vs. response in elite football. *Sport Performance & Science Reports*. 2025;(258), version 2.

## Why it was promoted

This conceptual paper offers a practical architecture for separating what training an athlete performed from how the athlete responded, across metabolic and neuromuscular systems.

## Research question

How can elite-football monitoring tools be organized so that load measures are not confused with acute responses or longer-term adaptations?

## Population and context

- Participants: No participant cohort; this is a conceptual/practice framework. `[pp. 2–3]`
- Sport and level: Elite football (soccer), with examples from team monitoring and return-to-play workflows. `[pp. 2, 10]`
- Training or return-to-play context: Routine microcycle monitoring and individualized return-to-play monitoring. `[p. 10]`
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Selective, author-curated technologies and references; not a systematic review or comparative validation study. `[pp. 2–5]`

## Study design and methods

1	# Lab 2C — Monitoring vs Testing: summary
2	
3	This full-course video is byte-identical (SHA-256) to the Lab 2C Free Version. The summary is therefore the same. It is based on the locally generated machine transcript, which has not been audio-reviewed. Timestamps refer to the MP4. The described workflow is the speaker’s example, not a validated clinical or training protocol.
4	
5	The speaker separates **monitoring**, which asks whether something changed over days or weeks, from **testing**, which asks whether capacity changed across a training phase or longer block. He calls the former a view of current status and the latter a view of progress. He emphasizes explaining that distinction to coaches and medical staff so a result is interpreted for the question it was collected to answer. (00:00–01:50)
6	
7	- Short-term monitoring may use rolling averages, exponentially weighted means, and recent baselines. Those methods can track acute status yet miss gradual drift because the reference itself moves. The speaker suggests comparing defined phases or time points when assessing longer-term change. (01:50–03:03)
8	- Define the question, choose the measurement, and set a schedule before collecting data. Testing should occur at planned points, with flexibility for acute questions such as a player's availability. (03:03–04:20)
9	- Tell coaches what is being evaluated, why, how often, when results will be delivered, and what different results would trigger. Discuss measurement error before treating a small difference as meaningful. (04:20–06:47)
10	- In a hamstring-force example, the speaker describes confirming test quality, obtaining a clinical assessment, assigning responsibility for an exposure adjustment, and setting a recheck. His stated timings and actions are an example of a decision pathway, not thresholds validated by this video. (06:47–07:42)
11	
12	The practical takeaway is to give monitoring and testing distinct questions, schedules, analysis methods, and action plans, and communicate those plans before a result creates pressure to act. (07:42–07:58)
13

1	# Podcast 2: Evidence Stacking
2	
3	**Source:** Locally transcribed course audio (about 18 minutes). Timestamps are approximate. The transcript is an automated draft and has not been checked against the audio.
4	
5	The central question is whether the staff have **enough independent, relevant information to act**. The speaker argues that a dramatic single result or initial impression should prompt further investigation, not settle a decision. An evidence stack combines the event or problem history, clinical findings where relevant, an athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance in the conditions the decision concerns.
6	
7	- **00:00–02:20 — Resist single-signal reactions.** The speaker frames evidence stacking as a way to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence.
8	- **02:20–10:30 — Soccer injury anecdote.** After an awkward knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL injuries, the speaker describes comparing the initial concern with imaging, clinical examination, movement, a known individual triple-hop baseline, agility, and subsequent training exposure. The point is to update the working assessment as different kinds of evidence arrive. The anecdote does not establish that a hop distance can diagnose an injury or clear an athlete to play.
9	- **10:30–17:35 — Hamstring return-to-play anecdote.** The speaker describes a second case in which clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at like-for-like speeds. He emphasizes closing the gap between controlled tests and the demands of the field. The reported return to competition is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.
10	- **17:35–18:15 — Leadership application.** Build within-athlete reference points, identify what each new measure adds, and protect the department from changing course on one isolated signal. Ask whether the stack is sufficiently complete for the specific decision.
11	
12	**Practical takeaway:** Define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that add distinct evidence. Medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions; these stories illustrate the reasoning approach rather than a clinical protocol.

1	# Lab 3B — Meeting Typology: summary
2	
3	Source: the downloaded Lab 3B MP4, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Times refer to the MP4. The transcript is machine-generated and has recognition errors, so ambiguous names and phrases have been omitted from this summary. This reports the speaker's recommendations; it does not independently establish their effectiveness.
4	
5	## Main point
6	
7	Select and announce a meeting's purpose before setting its agenda. The speaker argues that clearly named meeting modes improve preparation, protect creative work from premature decisions, and make decisions faster when the options are known. A staff meeting may include several modes, provided each segment has a stated purpose and expected output.
8	
9	## Meeting modes
10	
11	| Mode | Use it for | Structure and expected result |
12	| --- | --- | --- |
13	| **Decide** | A clear question with limited options | Pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review. The speaker connects this mode to the Kaigi format from Lab 3A. (01:03–02:14) |
14	| **Diagnose** | A known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain | Gather relevant perspectives and hypotheses, keep the discussion focused on a defined problem, and time-box contributions. The speaker suggests roughly 30 minutes as an example. If unresolved, assign a smaller group to gather more information, then schedule a later decision. (02:14–04:03) |
15	| **Inform** | Sharing updates and context | Keep the goal to information sharing. The speaker warns that such meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving. (04:37–05:02) |
16	| **Build** | Co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week | Give people room to contribute, consider psychological safety, and allow time to digest ideas. Some projects may need several meetings rather than one immediate decision. (05:34–06:18) |
17	
18	## Other formats and combinations
19	
20	- **Mixed staff meetings (04:03–04:37):** One agenda can move through inform, diagnose, and decide segments. Define the segment boundaries so participants know which kind of contribution is needed.
21	- **Operations meeting (05:02–05:34):** Use brief status updates, remove blockers, and assign ownership. An operations meeting may combine informing with quick decisions.
22	- **Retrospective or after-action review (06:18–07:08):** Review what happened, using a factual timeline, measures, and missing information. Keep the review blameless, then translate lessons into procedure changes. Examples mentioned include rehabilitation issues and a run of injuries.
23	
24	## Agenda and preparation
25	
26	Name the meeting type, define its purpose, specify timing, and state what output participants should produce. Participants should arrive prepared for the kind of meeting being held. The speaker says leaders can use meetings to gather perspectives that test their initial view before making a decision. (07:08–08:09)
27	
28	## Practical use
29	
30	For each agenda item, write one verb at the top: **decide, diagnose, inform, or build**. Add the question or topic, the expected output, a time limit, and any pre-reading. If diagnosis shows that more evidence is needed, assign the follow-up and schedule a separate decision point rather than letting the discussion drift.
31

Source: downloaded Lab 6D video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Examples involving athlete decisions illustrate a workflow; they are not clinical guidance.

## Main idea

The speaker asks teams to make the route from an observation to an action explicit, including who owns each step. He describes six stages: **data capture → quality control → analysis → interpretation → communication → decision and action**. (00:00–02:02)

## Five gaps to audit

1. **Dirty data, between capture and quality control.** Check that a collection protocol was followed and that anomalies are caught before data enters reports or a long-term database. Name an owner for this check. (02:02–02:59)
2. **Expertise, between quality control and analysis.** A reliable measurement can still be evaluated against an unsuitable threshold or without its normal context. Ask who sets and reviews the thresholds, including software defaults. (02:59–04:24)
3. **Interpretation, between analysis and meaning.** A number may reach a meeting without anyone saying what it means for the athlete or the decision. Excess data can also exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. (04:24–05:32)
4. **Communication, between interpretation and decision-maker.** Technical language can obscure the requested action. The speaker recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. (05:32–08:54)
5. **Authority, between recommendation and action.** Even a clear recommendation may be ignored if no formal decision gate or override process exists. The speaker calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions. (08:54–10:50)

**Practical takeaway:** Trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it. (10:52–12:11)

1	# Video Lab 6E — The Grey Zone: summary
2	
3	Source: downloaded Lab 6E video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. The return-to-activity phases are the speaker's example of team organization, not a patient-specific protocol.
4	
5	## Main idea
6	
7	The speaker calls the overlap between medical or physiotherapy staff and strength and performance staff the “grey zone.” He argues that differences in training, priorities, timelines, and risk tolerance become a problem when the overlap has no agreed operating rules. The leader's task is to make responsibilities and decisions explicit while preserving each discipline's perspective. (00:00–02:44)
8	
9	## Organizing the overlap
10	
11	- Consider the actual practitioners' skills and willingness to collaborate before assigning roles. A job title alone does not establish who is best equipped for a specific task. (02:44–03:59; 06:33–07:11)
12	- Agree on the phases, decision points, measures, and criteria the department will use. The speaker describes one model with medical leadership early in rehabilitation and strength staff taking operational responsibility for return to running, while both continue to contribute. He says this division should change when personnel skills warrant it. (03:59–07:11)
13	- Name an operational owner for each phase, define what that person can change independently, and state which decisions require escalation. Also specify who must be informed and how quickly when an athlete's plan changes. (07:11–10:43)
14	
15	## Team exercise
16	
17	Walk through one rehabilitation case twice: once from the physiotherapist's priorities and constraints, and once from the strength coach's. Compare the accounts at each handoff, then agree on ownership, progression criteria, information to transfer, change authority, and notification rules. (10:43–13:02)
18	
19	**Practical takeaway:** Make the shared work visible and assign responsibility at each transition so the athlete's plan can pass between disciplines without relying on assumptions. (12:12–13:02)
20

14	# Know a Sprint Drill's Origin Before You Copy It
15	
16	**What it is** — Moyer's case against "monkey see, monkey do" programming: coaches lift a drill from social media or a clinic and **plug it in without knowing who it was built for, what problem it solved, and where it sat in the original training program**. His Live 1 phrasing: *"everything works — it just has its place."* Knowing a method's origin is what he calls a **"bullshit barometer"**: when a claim does not match the population or purpose the method came from, you can see it.
17	
18	**Why it works** — A drill is a solution to a specific problem in a specific system. Strip away the system and you keep the form but lose the reason: the fault it corrected, the athlete level it assumed, the phase it belonged to, the dose. The principle is sound general appraisal logic. Moyer's stronger add-on — that "there is literally nothing new in sports science" and modern sprint research mostly rediscovers 1960s–80s Soviet work — is **his opinion**, argued by example (pawback, thigh angular velocity), not demonstrated.
19	
20	**When to apply** — A position coach brings in a viral drill. A new staff member wants to import a program from their last school. Any time a drill's justification is "an elite sprinter does it." Ask three questions: who was it designed for, what fault or quality did it target, and what came before and after it in that program.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to dismiss new work because it is new, or to treat old sources as automatically superior; Moyer's own history lessons carry factual slips (see the digest in the ingest report), which is the point applied back to him. Origin is also not the only test: a drill with an unknown origin can still be judged on whether it changes the target fault on film. Use origin to *frame* the question, and outcome on your own athletes to *answer* it.
23	
24	**Example** — Pawback drills. Moyer traces them from Soviet texts through Yessis to current 1080-sprint variants. A staff that knows the drill was meant to train the late-swing, down-and-back action for athletes who land in front of the hips will use it for those athletes, and will not give it to a lineman whose problem is acceleration posture.
25	
26	**Related** — [[principle--judge-a-sprint-method-by-the-population-it-was-built-on]] — the same appraisal applied to research populations.

# Know a Sprint Drill's Origin Before You Copy It

**What it is** — Moyer's case against "monkey see, monkey do" programming: coaches lift a drill from social media or a clinic and **plug it in without knowing who it was built for, what problem it solved, and where it sat in the original training program**. His Live 1 phrasing: *"everything works — it just has its place."* Knowing a method's origin is what he calls a **"bullshit barometer"**: when a claim does not match the population or purpose the method came from, you can see it.

**Why it works** — A drill is a solution to a specific problem in a specific system. Strip away the system and you keep the form but lose the reason: the fault it corrected, the athlete level it assumed, the phase it belonged to, the dose. The principle is sound general appraisal logic. Moyer's stronger add-on — that "there is literally nothing new in sports science" and modern sprint research mostly rediscovers 1960s–80s Soviet work — is **his opinion**, argued by example (pawback, thigh angular velocity), not demonstrated.

**When to apply** — A position coach brings in a viral drill. A new staff member wants to import a program from their last school. Any time a drill's justification is "an elite sprinter does it." Ask three questions: who was it designed for, what fault or quality did it target, and what came before and after it in that program.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to dismiss new work because it is new, or to treat old sources as automatically superior; Moyer's own history lessons carry factual slips (see the digest in the ingest report), which is the point applied back to him. Origin is also not the only test: a drill with an unknown origin can still be judged on whether it changes the target fault on film. Use origin to *frame* the question, and outcome on your own athletes to *answer* it.

**Example** — Pawback drills. Moyer traces them from Soviet texts through Yessis to current 1080-sprint variants. A staff that knows the drill was meant to train the late-swing, down-and-back action for athletes who land in front of the hips will use it for those athletes, and will not give it to a lineman whose problem is acceleration posture.

**Related** — [[principle--judge-a-sprint-method-by-the-population-it-was-built-on]] — the same appraisal applied to research populations.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part III, staff should "begin with the athlete question or problem, then select a measurement tool" rather than starting from the equipment on hand (00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. Fits directly onto Baylor's Applied Performance data dictionary gap: the current dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. This principle gives that gap a specific fix order: name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# CM2: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum

**What it is** — A four-stage shared map Weber uses to describe where an athlete sits in a program, so staff across strength and conditioning, rehab, and sports science can communicate quickly without re-litigating vocabulary. The stages: **Control** (single-joint, isolated activation, used early in rehab or with an athlete who cannot yet sequence joints), **Movement** (multi-joint, integrated patterns that are "viable and repeatable... without falling apart"), **Capacity** (building the "engine": volume and tolerance for work, where "a lot of athletes live for large parts of the year"), and **Maximum** (short exposures to peak speed, force, or power once capacity is built) (Lab 1A transcript, 00:06:05–00:08:32). Athletes move forward when ready and back to an earlier stage when needed. Weber names it twice in the same recording, once as "CM2" (00:06:10) and once as "STM squared" (00:09:21); the automated transcript may have mis-heard one or both labels, so neither name should be treated as verified without checking the audio.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is coordination, not physiology: a large staff (athlete, performance manager, several S&C coaches, athletic trainers, physios, sports science staff) needs "a very, very simple language... to allow people to move quickly and not get bogged down" (00:08:32–00:09:00). Placing an athlete on the map ("he's not moving that well, we need to drop him back to control") gives a leader a one-line status update across disciplines without needing agreement on deeper theory.

**When to apply** — As a discussion shorthand in interdisciplinary handoffs (rehab to performance, performance to sport coach) when the question is "where is this athlete in the process" rather than a specific numeric threshold. Maps loosely onto the Vermeil hierarchy already used in Eric's own course material (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) [method-baseline.md, Strength and power], so it could sit alongside rather than replace that existing shared vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber presents this as one example teams can adapt, not a validated developmental model ("I made my [CM2] thing up. You don't have to use that," 00:09:26–00:09:31). It carries no criteria for how to know an athlete has met a stage's bar, no timelines, and no evidence it improves outcomes; it is a communication convention, not an assessment protocol. Do not substitute it for Baylor's own testing/reassessment criteria [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment].

**Example** — Weber's illustration: an athlete in early rehab who cannot yet sequence multiple joints stays in single-joint Control work (e.g., isolated clam exercises) rather than progressing to complex movement drills; once that control is established, the priority becomes "getting moving" as fast as safely possible rather than lingering in isolated work (00:07:07–00:07:44).

**Related** — [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the ordering rule this map is built to support.

# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that most performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department "chases noise and calls it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). Directly usable against Baylor's own documented gap: current GPS/VALD workflow SOPs are described by Eric's own gap analysis as "generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail" outside the Catapult workflow [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2] — this audit's Step 1–3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" and his contrast with himself ("I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models... that's me because I want to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the companion audit that adds who-does-what-with-it. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics behind Step 2. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the chain this audit sets up (procedure to reliability to confidence to defensible decisions).
