# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that most performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department "chases noise and calls it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). Directly usable against Baylor's own documented gap: current GPS/VALD workflow SOPs are described by Eric's own gap analysis as "generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail" outside the Catapult workflow [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2] — this audit's Step 1–3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" and his contrast with himself ("I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models... that's me because I want to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. # Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own outranks any device they might buy next: "it's the most powerful piece of performance tech you own," yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example: "I've been a strength and conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). A department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. Reality-checks cleanly against Eric's own practice: he already reports running Python-adjacent workflows and building dashboards, and his gap analysis explicitly names "sport-specific data dictionaries" and "Baylor-specific technology workflows" as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3] — work that depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just the vendor tools.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code, only that the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.

**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — arguing this "reduce[s] ambiguity and give[s] both leaders and staff more room for focused work" (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure, which is what frees attention for harder problems.

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is "worth the paperwork": onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing the credential-vault protocol his own gap analysis already flags as missing [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. It also gives a concrete rationale for the intern curriculum's stated goal of teaching "the how" alongside "the why" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1] — the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). A department whose SOPs are current can answer yes; Baylor's own Playbook shows the failure mode Weber warns against, since its NordBord section still documents a full roster-style collection protocol that was never updated after the practice was retired for football in 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8] — the procedure fell out of sync with the decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, not judgments of a person's worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is "does this person need more knowledge, more engagement, or both." Weber's advice to pick mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that it is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, "rather than a person's worth" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).

**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement "may limit a team's progress" (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise: have staff list five things that could derail the department, as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks (00:00–02:36).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is diagnostic, not just motivational: a CPD conversation reveals two different things at once — whether someone needs support to grow, and whether they are actually interested in progressing. That distinction maps directly onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): a staff member who has no CPD activity might be a knowledge gap, a motivation gap, or both, and the conversation is how a leader tells which.

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. Fits naturally into Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing: "he proposes asking staff about continuing professional development and inviting brief presentations about recent learning" as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

# Match Mentors to the Sport, Not Just the Discipline

**What it is** — Weber's stated preference, for performance-sport roles specifically, is to choose mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments," rather than mentors who share a technical discipline but not the sport context (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18).

**Why it works** — Weber does not give a mechanism beyond his own stated preference; the implicit reasoning is that comparable-sport experience carries tacit knowledge (competition calendar pressures, roster size, sport-specific injury patterns) that a mentor from an unrelated sport or setting would not have, even with equal or greater technical depth in the discipline itself.

**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a technically strong mentor from an unrelated sport and one with direct comparable-sport background. Directly relevant to Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] — this heuristic argues for weighting the football-specific voices in that mentoring structure, not just the general sport-science ones.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between sport-matched and discipline-matched mentors, and no guidance for cases where no sport-matched mentor is available. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.

**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for staff to "practice leadership before receiving the title" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use over roughly two decades (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber's implicit argument is that adopting a technology before an environment's procedures, staff skill, and interpretive norms have matured to match it recreates the tech-rich/procedure-poor problem he names in Lab 1C (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]): the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist.

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not "is this tool valid" but "has this tool, and my staff's ability to use it, matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost."

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and "maturity" here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption; earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline: "he contrasts early users of new tools with GPS, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use" (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

# Data to Information to Knowledge to Wisdom

**What it is** — Weber uses the standard data-information-knowledge-wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy to argue that storing measurements and building dashboards (data, information) does not, by itself, help a department make a decision (knowledge, wisdom); each step up the hierarchy requires additional interpretive work, not just more collection (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 03:27–04:42).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism connects directly to communication capacity: a coach or medical colleague handed a complex dashboard is left to do the interpretation themselves, which he illustrates with a "pick-up 52" analogy — see [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — meaning the recipient is handed a scattered deck and asked to reassemble it into an answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44).

**When to apply** — Reviewing any recurring report or dashboard against the question "does this hand the reader data, or does it hand them an answer." # Start From the Recipient's Question, Not the Full Dashboard ("Pick-Up 52")

**What it is** — Weber's "pick-up 52" analogy: handing a coach or medical colleague a complex, unfiltered dashboard is like scattering a deck of 52 cards on the floor and asking them to pick it up and make sense of it themselves (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44). His alternative: the communicator should begin with the recipient's actual question and decide which information is relevant to that question before presenting anything, specifying the equipment, standards, and reporting format up front (07:44–08:54).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is that a dashboard which "leaves the coach or medical colleague to do the interpretation" transfers cognitive work to the person least equipped to reconcile multiple measures against each other, and least likely to know which differences are within normal error. Framing the report around a stated question forces the practitioner, who has that context, to do the reconciliation once instead of the recipient doing it every time.

**When to apply** — Designing any recurring coach- or medical-facing report or dashboard, especially where Baylor's own gap analysis already flags standardized reporting templates as unbuilt [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. Also useful when a new coach or staff member joins and needs to be told what they will receive and why, matching the same communication checklist Lab 2C recommends for monitoring and testing (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a design heuristic for the recipient-facing layer of reporting; it does not argue against keeping a full, granular dataset available to the practitioners who need it. Weber gives no template for how to identify "the recipient's question" when it has not been stated, only that it should be established before building the report.

**Example** — Weber's own SpeedSig product classification, described as reducing many measures into a simpler signal while keeping detail available "for those who need it," is his illustration of the practice — offered as a product example, not independent evidence that the underlying classification is clinically or competitively valid (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 08:54–10:39).

**Related** — [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — the model this heuristic operationalizes. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parallel communication checklist for monitoring and testing reports.

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — Protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber pairs this with a statistical-interpretation point: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. Directly relevant to Baylor's own force-plate protocol: the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is exactly the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability — but Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test (the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues) [method-baseline.md Tensions #5], which is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run; a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19) — both symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.

# The Constraint on 2020s Practitioners Is Vetting Information, Not Finding More of It

**What it is** — Weber's historical framing, opening the course: sport science and strength-and-conditioning practice grew from Milo of Croton's progressive overload through research institutes, periodization theory, biomechanics, and increasing specialization, then accelerated further with GPS/inertial tracking, force measurement, online coaching content, academic reviews, and social media (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 00:00–09:06). His claim: for practitioners entering the field now, the binding constraint is "vetting, filtering, and integrating information," not finding more of it, in contrast to his own earlier reliance on academic sources and experienced coaches (09:06–11:41). He extends this to AI specifically: useful for preliminary research and helping a skilled coder work faster, but short AI summaries "can strip away nuance," and practitioners who lack the underlying skill may overtrust AI-generated code, training plans, or rehabilitation plans (same range).

**Why it works** — This is Weber's own historical narrative and personal contrast between "his day" and now, not a documented survey of practitioner information behavior; the mechanism (more channels producing more unfiltered volume) is plausible but not measured here.

**When to apply** — As a framing device when deciding how to train newer staff or interns: the emphasis shifts from "find more sources" toward "build a filter" — knowing which claims to trust, which social-media clips to discount, and which AI outputs need independent verification before use. Consistent with Eric's own course material's stated skepticism of "viral clip" training trends and its caution that a clip is "just a brief snapshot" stripped of context [method-baseline.md, Philosophy and decision principles].

**When NOT to apply** — Treat this as Weber's opinion and personal history, not as an evidenced claim about how practitioners as a group actually behave; the transcript is machine-generated and historical names/dates in this section should be checked against the audio before being repeated as fact (course README caveat). It should not be cited as a finding that AI tools are unreliable in general, only as Weber's specific caution about unverified AI-generated training or rehab content in the hands of someone without the underlying skill to check it.

**Example** — Weber's own closing framing for Part I: growth in technology and information has changed how performance departments operate, which he uses to set up the course's later modules on staff capability and decision structure (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 11:41–12:19).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the staff-capability framework this claim sets up. [[framework--rogers-adoption-curve-for-perf-tech]] — the companion framing for judging a specific technology's maturity.

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples: calling a lower countermovement-jump result "neurological fatigue," or a GPS change "tissue stress" — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Collapsing the distinction lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. Applies directly to Baylor's mRSI-as-readiness-marker practice: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen objective readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example: what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02) — the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from "what do we have" to "what does it produce and who acts on it." The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves.

**Why it works (strategy vs. tactics)** — Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to Baylor's own department model, where Applied Performance is explicitly a support/advisory role feeding decisions that Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine make [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of that shared workflow, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model].

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where the "decision" cell of this matrix gets formalized.

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from "what do we have" to "what does it produce and who acts on it." The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves.

**Why it works (strategy vs. tactics)** — Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to Baylor's own department model, where Applied Performance is explicitly a support/advisory role feeding decisions that Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine make [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of that shared workflow, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model].

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. # Strategy Is the Highway, Tactics Are Changing Lanes

**What it is** — Weber's delegation model: **strategy** is the department's direction, standards, and the key questions it cares about, described as "the highway"; **tactics** are the day-to-day choices staff make within that direction (which tool to deploy, how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure, how to respond to what they see), described as "changing lanes" (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1–2). The stated goal is to give staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (p.2). He restates the same model in Webinar 3 Part III as a direct delegation rule: the leader names the destination and boundaries, staff choose tactics within them, with more discretion given to an experienced colleague than a new hire, and explicit criteria for which decisions must be escalated (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is that without a named boundary, staff either wait for permission on every tactical choice (killing responsiveness) or drift from department standards one small decision at a time (killing alignment). Naming the highway once, in writing, removes the need to re-negotiate it for every individual tactical call.

**When to apply** — Structuring how much autonomy a staff member has over test selection, session adjustments, or reporting choices, especially as a department scales past a size where informal alignment happens naturally. Gives a concrete vocabulary for Eric's own department-model gap: the Playbook's stated peer-department framing for Applied Performance is not fully reconciled with the "support staff" framing that appears elsewhere in the same corpus [method-baseline.md Tensions #2] — naming the specific highway (standards, questions Applied Performance owns) versus the lanes (tactical choices left to individual practitioners) is a direct way to resolve that ambiguity in practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no method for determining where the highway's boundaries should sit for a given department or decision type; that judgment call is left entirely to the leader. It is also not a substitute for the formal escalation criteria a decision gate provides (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) when the stakes are high enough to need a documented pass/fail/borderline threshold rather than a general delegation boundary.

**Example** — Weber's contrast: an experienced colleague gets wider tactical discretion than a new hire under the same strategic direction, with explicit agreement on which decisions must be escalated rather than decided independently (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Related** — [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the audit this delegation model is embedded in. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the more formal structure for higher-stakes decisions. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the companion communication rules from the same Webinar 3 material.

# Monitoring vs. Testing

**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks cannot catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness — a real tension worth naming against Eric's own baseline, which states a preference for "weekly tracking... over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early" [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved — the two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his 12% RFD example and similar single-number illustrations are heuristics, not transferable thresholds; the actual analysis method appropriate for a given metric depends on the test and context (p.2, and see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].

**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.

# A Rolling Baseline Can Hide the Exact Long-Term Drift You Are Trying to Catch

**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" — because the reference point (the rolling average itself) moves along with the slow change you would need to detect (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).

**Why it works** — A rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over eight weeks, a 7- or 14-day rolling average tracks that drift and never flags it as a deviation, because the "baseline" itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change.

**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question ("has this athlete's capacity actually improved this block"). This is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and Eric's stated preference for weekly tracking to catch plateaus.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.

**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.

# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC

**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. This is a direct, stated gap in Eric's own corpus: mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], but no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus — Weber's framework would treat that as the non-negotiable missing step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that "you don't need to become a statistician here" but the minimum thinking is still required (p.1); this framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. His "greater than MDC / greater than SWC" examples are heuristics, not universal calculation rules — the appropriate method depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary, 02:27–03:53).

**Example** — Weber's rate-of-force-development (RFD) case: a 12% difference may be uninformative if it falls within the metric's own local measurement variability, because execution consistency, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences create large swings in calculated RFD; see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response (pp.2–3). The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.

**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] — the specific fix for a noisy metric like RFD. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — where reliability is first introduced as a step-2 check.

# When a Metric Is Noisy, Widen the Threshold, Tighten the Protocol, or Pick a Different Metric

**What it is** — Weber's three-option response when a metric shows high inherent variability, illustrated with rate of force development (RFD): "the takeaway is not 'never use RFD.' The takeaway is: when a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose a more stable metric for decision gates" (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.2). He attributes RFD's typical noise to three sources: execution-consistency demands, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences that produce large swings in the calculated value (p.2).

**Why it works** — This gives a leader three genuinely different levers instead of one binary (use it or drop it): widening the decision threshold accepts the noise and raises the bar for calling a change real; tightening the protocol (standardizing onset detection, warm-up, instructions) reduces the noise itself; switching metrics sidesteps the problem by choosing a more stable measure of a similar underlying quality. Which lever is right depends on whether the noise comes from the measurement process (fixable by protocol) or is closer to genuine biological/mechanical variability (better handled by a wider threshold or a different metric).

**When to apply** — Any time a metric is flagged as unreliable during the reliability-vs-sensitivity audit (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]), rather than either dropping the metric outright or continuing to use it with an unexamined threshold. Directly applicable to any force-plate "fluffy" metric in Baylor's own reporting framework (peak power, average power, RFD), which the adopted Hawkin Dynamics ODSF metric-selection framework already flags as needing "a specific, defensible rationale" before inclusion [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this heuristic is the concrete follow-up once a metric like RFD is found to be noisy in-house.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not say how to choose between the three levers for a given case, only that one of them is the right response to noise; this is a decision menu, not a decision rule. It also does not apply to a metric whose problem is not noise but validity (measuring the wrong construct entirely) — that is a different failure mode, addressed by [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]].

**Example** — Weber's stated leadership framing for this whole statistical package: "if staff are using tests with unknown reliability, then when they bring you a number, there is no foundation for trust. Statistical rigour gives you credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, decision gates that work" (p.2).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the diagnostic this heuristic responds to. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit's own procedure-first fix for a different but related problem (undocumented protocol).

# When a Metric Is Noisy, Widen the Threshold, Tighten the Protocol, or Pick a Different Metric

**What it is** — Weber's three-option response when a metric shows high inherent variability, illustrated with rate of force development (RFD): "the takeaway is not 'never use RFD.' The takeaway is: when a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose a more stable metric for decision gates" (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.2). He attributes RFD's typical noise to three sources: execution-consistency demands, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences that produce large swings in the calculated value (p.2).

Which lever is right depends on whether the noise comes from the measurement process (fixable by protocol) or is closer to genuine biological/mechanical variability (better handled by a wider threshold or a different metric).

# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision: does staff have "enough independent, relevant information to act" (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is "one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance" (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism, illustrated with two anecdotes (a soccer knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL history, and a hamstring return-to-play case), is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Combining them and updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive (Podcast 2 summary, 02:20–17:35).

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). Gives a concrete practice for a tension in Eric's own material: the course transcripts argue "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3] — evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach; they do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury or that any specific stack of tests can clear an athlete to play, and medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions outside this framework's scope (Podcast 2 summary, 18:15 caveat). It also does not specify how many independent streams are "enough" for a given decision — that judgment is left to the practitioner.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.

**Related** — [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the single-measurement discipline this framework scales up. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where a completed evidence stack feeds a formal go/hold/stop decision. [[principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]] — the reliability discipline each stream in the stack still needs individually.

# The Kaigi Decision Meeting

**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow; forcing preparation and concise contributions works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.

**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone — aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Kaigi-transcript summary, 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that a decision meeting has different requirements from sharing information, creating solutions, or educating staff (00:00–02:18); using kaigi structure to force a decision before the options are actually narrowed to two or three, or before enough evidence exists, will produce a fast but poorly grounded call. His own Go/No-Go numbers (roughly 15–17 staff, under 30 seconds per player, 20-minute follow-up) are his example's parameters, not validated operating thresholds or a recommended clinical protocol.

**When NOT to apply (continued)** — See [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for the broader set of meeting modes; kaigi is specifically the "decide" mode and should not be reached for when the actual need is "diagnose" or "build."

**Example** — Weber's stalled-meeting rescue: when a broader problem-solving discussion stalls, explicitly announce the switch to decision mode, give it a fixed short window (his example: 10 minutes), and require a stated decision, an owner, and a documented outcome before the group moves on (12:14–13:23).

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping this format requires. [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this format sits inside. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — the companion presentation format for the evidence brought into a kaigi-style meeting.

# The Kaigi Decision Meeting

**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow; forcing preparation and concise contributions works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.

**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone — aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Kaigi-transcript summary, 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that a decision meeting has different requirements from sharing information, creating solutions, or educating staff (00:00–02:18); using kaigi structure to force a decision before the options are actually narrowed to two or three, or before enough evidence exists, will produce a fast but poorly grounded call. **Example** — Weber's stalled-meeting rescue: when a broader problem-solving discussion stalls, explicitly announce the switch to decision mode, give it a fixed short window (his example: 10 minutes), and require a stated decision, an owner, and a documented outcome before the group moves on (12:14–13:23).

# The Decision Log: Action, Owner, Due Date, Review

**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format: the meeting-typology "decide" mode requires "an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review" (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with "one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point, recorded in the decision log" (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with "the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update" (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down "creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed" (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). Without a record, a verbal decision is subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). Directly usable as a template for Baylor's own return-to-play and technology-adoption decisions, where Eric's own gap analysis already notes that no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol exists in writing [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — a decision log does not supply the criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale — Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

**Example** — Weber's stoplight-storytelling version adds one more requirement to the same four fields: "every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date" (Lab 3C summary, 05:51–06:23) — closing the loophole of an ambiguous "wait and see" outcome with no owner attached.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running "decide" structure on a "diagnose" problem, or vice versa). Fits directly onto Baylor's HHPR 5355 course structure and any Applied Performance staff meeting; the retrospective mode in particular gives a named structure to the kind of after-the-fact review Eric's own material shows happening informally around training decisions [method-baseline.md, Periodization and programming].

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs — that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda, and a leader using meetings to "gather perspectives that test their initial view before deciding" (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, which is a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.

**Example** — Weber's retrospective example: reviewing "a run of injuries" with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).

**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the fuller "decide" mode structure. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — a presentation format built for the "decide" mode specifically. [[heuristic--time-box-recurring-meetings]] — the time-discipline this typology assumes throughout.

# Stoplight Storytelling

**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). Forcing one chart and one request removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts: adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.

**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's two-minute benchmark and single-chart rule are explicitly not meant for novel or complex issues, which he says may need pre-reading or a dedicated meeting instead (06:23–06:43); forcing a genuinely complex, multi-variable problem into stoplight format risks the same false simplicity the framework is designed to avoid elsewhere (see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]). The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.

**Example** — Weber's practical template, stated directly: question, then green/amber/red status, then one clear chart with uncertainty and supporting context, then requested direction, then owner/due date/review (07:54 close, restated as the lab's summary template).

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the closing record this format requires. [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the meeting format this presentation style is built to feed. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the caution against over-simplifying a genuinely complex decision.
