# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill

**What it is** — Weber treats running a meeting as a deliberate developmental exercise: giving a staff member ownership of a meeting's structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability builds confidence and practical leadership skill (Lab 3D summary, 00:46–02:25). His own example: assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist. Implementation notes: define the meeting's purpose, keep an agenda, hold time limits and agreed decision boundaries, and record an owner/action/due-date/review for each output, while giving the facilitator room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy (02:25–03:11; see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]). For less confident speakers, start small: one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time, and deliberately track who contributes so quieter staff are invited in with advance notice of when they will present (03:11–05:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is graduated exposure: a staff member who is given a bounded, low-stakes facilitation role (one slide, one topic) practices the mechanics of running structured discussion without the full weight of an open-ended meeting, then earns larger scope as competence shows. This mirrors the knowledge x behaviour matrix's developmental use (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): meeting ownership is a concrete vehicle for moving someone along the knowledge axis.

**When to apply** — Identifying a staff member or intern ready for more responsibility, or building a structured on-ramp for a quieter staff member who has relevant expertise but does not volunteer it. Fits Baylor's proposed intern curriculum goal of a "professional portfolio of real work products" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — running an assigned meeting segment, with the agenda and decision log as artifacts, is one such work product.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for judging when a staff member is ready to move from a one-slide, one-topic assignment to a full meeting; that judgment is left to the assigning leader. This heuristic also assumes the leader is willing to accept the facilitation being less polished at first than if the leader ran it themselves — it is a deliberate trade of short-term efficiency for staff development.

**Example** — Weber's advancement path: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot; increase responsibility from there (03:11–05:09).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the broader developmental framework this practice serves. [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the companion senior-leadership practice from the same lab.

domain: performance-technology-and-leadership

topic: forcing a case against the group's preferred plan
category: [meetings, leadership, decision-gate]

# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide

**What it is** — Weber's practice for senior leaders: state a problem, then pause to hear staff views before offering an opinion, so the leader's own view does not anchor the discussion; he sometimes assigns someone to prepare an opposing case with evidence, and treats the resulting debate as a way to test his own assumptions before deciding (Lab 3D summary, 06:14–08:49). He restates the same practice in Podcast 6 with two named devices for structured dissent: the "tenth man" idea from *World War Z* (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation) and Edward de Bono's "six hats," used to deliberately examine a decision apart from the pressure around it and then from the athlete's or other stakeholders' point of view (Podcast 6 summary, 01:42–08:04). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure, and a leader who speaks first sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them. Formally assigning the dissenting role removes the social cost: the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.

**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. Weber's own recurring calf-injury anecdote (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is his illustration of what happens when dissent has no formal channel and instead depends on finding the right messenger after the fact (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion; using it for every routine call would slow decision-making without adding much value. The film and historical references (World War Z, six hats) are illustrations of the practice, not evidence for its effectiveness in a performance department, and the calf-injury anecdote is a personal account that does not establish the training change's actual effect on injury rates.

**Example** — Weber's own account: a coach who "listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail," rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).

**Related** — [[heuristic--assign-meeting-ownership-to-develop-staff]] — the companion staff-development practice from the same lab. [[heuristic--review-the-system-on-a-schedule]] — the broader practice of scheduling this kind of challenge proactively rather than only after a problem appears.

# Tighten One Recurring Meeting to Protect Staff Capacity

**What it is** — Weber's "20 minutes of discipline" structure for recurring operational decision meetings: send information roughly 24 hours in advance so attendees can read and consider it, state the required outcome at the start, keep discussion to what is working, what is not, and what needs to change, name who decides when a decision is needed, close with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update, start and stop on time (a visible timer where useful), and route useful off-topic items to a "parking lot" with an owner and next step (Podcast 3 summary, 07:20–11:11). "20 minutes" is his target for suitable routine meetings, not a limit he applies to every discussion (00:00–01:28). His challenge to the listener is to tighten just **one** recurring meeting, then ask whether anything valuable was lost and whether its outputs improved (12:16–16:44).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is capacity protection: time saved in a tightened recurring meeting is time preserved for analysis, project work, and the training/treatment schedule itself (00:00–01:28, 02:58–04:24). Pre-reading and a stated required outcome shift the meeting's actual work (absorbing context, forming an initial view) to before the room convenes, so the meeting itself is spent on discussion and decision rather than briefing.

**When to apply** — Any standing weekly or daily operational meeting that has grown past its original purpose (a status update that has become a discussion, a discussion that has become a debate). Weber's own examples of what a tightened format looks like: a planning meeting using short timed rounds to collect responses to three questions from five people (about 40 minutes, described as preparing months of work), and short daily stand-ups surfacing completed work, next work, and blockers (01:28–02:58, 11:11–11:26).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber explicitly distinguishes this format from brainstorming and relationship-building, and recommends preparation, smaller pieces, and small multidisciplinary groups for genuinely complex problems rather than forcing them into a tight recurring slot (12:16–15:31); see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" mode is the wrong fit. His efficiency claims (the 40-minute planning meeting "prepared months of work") are his own account, not measured against an alternative.

**Example** — Weber's own operational rule for the parking lot: an off-topic issue that is nonetheless useful gets a named owner and a next step, so it is captured without derailing the meeting's actual agenda (10:08–11:11).

**Related** — [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this time-discipline applies within. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the closing record this format shares with the course's other meeting formats.

# Agree Which Channel Carries What, and When, Before the Pressure Arrives

**What it is** — Weber's set of communication rules meant to be settled in advance rather than negotiated in the moment: specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected on it; for injuries specifically, state in advance when the coach receives a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may follow; agree the timing and form of post-training reports, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats; mark messages by urgency or purpose; and make meeting invitations state their objective, length, and required preparation, with project assignments stating the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult, plus expected response times (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 06:11–10:09). In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about "training load" from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).

**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. Gives concrete structure to Eric's own department's stated advisory role: Applied Performance's job is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence.

**Example** — Weber's military-analogy caution in Part I: he explicitly warns that military and sport stakes differ, using the analogy only to illustrate that rehearsed communication routines let a team act without inventing a process under pressure — in one AFL case, coach and performance staff changed a session live during play because they shared enough technical language to estimate consequences for specific players in real time (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 05:05–09:03).

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this set of rules extends. [[heuristic--translate-metrics-into-coaches-vocabulary]] — the vocabulary-specific version of this same discipline. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation-boundary companion from the same Webinar.

# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision

**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gap** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence, which he frames as a shared responsibility ("practitioners share responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information"); **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). Naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that "good work isn't landing" into a specific, auditable question: which of the five links actually failed.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1) — a useful test to run against Baylor's own KPI-threshold principle, which is named as a departmental operating principle but has no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol documented anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play].

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).

**Example** — Weber's authority-gap distinction: overriding a technical recommendation is "sometimes necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.

**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gap is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.

# The Encoding Problem: Same Athlete, Different Lens

**What it is** — Weber's observation that different professional groups reviewing the same athlete and the same data routinely see different problems, not because they disagree about the facts, but because those facts are "encoded" differently by discipline: a physiotherapist sees tissue tolerance, healing, and rehabilitation progress; a medical practitioner sees health status and risk; a strength and conditioning coach sees readiness, output, and return-to-performance demands; a sports scientist sees load, exposure, and the numerical pathway to competition; a coach sees availability (can the athlete train, can the athlete play) (Module_6B_Part_A PDF p.1). His proposed fix is a written, shared case framework: document how a given scenario (his example: a hamstring injury) will be assessed, the checkpoints, expected timing, and who acts at each handoff, built collaboratively with medical, physiotherapy, strength, and sport science staff so each group also learns what the others do (Video Lab 6B summary, 02:44–06:37; PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism: when staff understand what other disciplines are doing, "departments become less defensive, less territorial, and more collaborative... staff are more willing to share information, raise concerns early, and adjust without fear or confusion" (PDF p.1). He is explicit this is not about eliminating disciplinary difference — healthy technical disagreement should be "respected and examined" — but about ensuring differences operate inside a shared structure rather than each discipline silently running its own model (PDF p.2).

**When to apply** — Any interdisciplinary case (injury, load management, return-to-play) where different departments have historically produced different read-outs of the same athlete without a documented shared plan. Directly names the coordination Baylor's own department model already implies but does not fully specify in writing: Applied Performance's stated role is to enable Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Department model], and this framework is a concrete method (a written pathway, checkpoints, and criteria per case type) for making that enabling role operational rather than aspirational.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber distinguishes healthy technical challenge from a staff member working outside the agreed process; the framework is meant to protect the former and surface the latter, not to suppress disagreement (PDF p.2). His own anecdote — presenting injury-risk evidence that was new and unfamiliar to a coach and doctor who lacked a shared framework for understanding it, followed by the predicted injuries occurring — is a personal account illustrating a communication failure, not evidence that the specific injury-risk claim itself was correct (PDF p.2).

**Example** — Weber's own summary of the stakes: "correct data is not enough. If the leader cannot get the information understood across disciplines, the work has failed at the level that matters most" (PDF p.2).

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the upstream framework this problem sits inside (specifically the language gap). [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]] — the direct follow-on once an encoding gap has been identified. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — the applied version of this same shared-framework idea for medical/performance overlap.

# Constant Translation Is a Diagnostic Signal: Replace It With Education

**What it is** — Weber's argument that repeatedly explaining the same concept to different stakeholders (medical, physiotherapy, strength and conditioning, sports science, coaching) is not just a communication cost but a symptom that the environment has not been educated to a common operating understanding (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1). He calls this a genuine "cognitive cost" and "performance leak inside the organisation," since it drains time and attention that could go to higher-level problems (p.1). His prescribed response: avoid translation where possible and replace it with education, treating a recurring need to re-explain the same idea as useful diagnostic information rather than an inconvenience to absorb (p.1). He offers two implementation routes depending on context: drawing a firm, clearly stated line in how the system will operate (faster, more likely to create friction, appropriate when confusion is already embedded), or building alignment through workshops, internal CPD, and structured educational sessions (slower, better suited where there is more time or openness) (p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism ties this directly to the discipline-equals-freedom chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed... that frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (p.1). He also introduces a leadership-honesty distinction: **technical leadership** (a leader with enough depth to personally teach the framework) versus **structural leadership** (a leader who instead ensures the right technical people are in place to do it); either is legitimate, but "technical coherence cannot be left to chance. Someone must own it" (p.2).

**When to apply** — Whenever the same concept has to be re-explained to different stakeholders more than once or twice in a season, treat that repetition itself as the signal to intervene, not just the individual instance to answer. Relevant to Baylor's own proposed intern curriculum, which already commits to sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3] — this heuristic argues those sessions exist specifically to eliminate a recurring translation cost, not just to build general awareness.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that some explanation will always be necessary, particularly concise executive-level updates for coaches; the goal is reducing unnecessary translation, not eliminating all of it (p.1). This heuristic also assumes the leader has honestly audited whether they personally have the technical depth to lead the education, or need to bring in someone who does (p.2); skipping that self-audit risks a leader attempting technical leadership they cannot actually deliver.

**Example** — Weber's pelvis/clam case: a rehabilitation issue had been framed narrowly as a strength problem (poor frontal-plane pelvis control treated with isolated abduction work), until technically grounded leadership reframed it as a motor-control problem, demonstrating the athletes were already strong enough in isolation and that the real issue was stabilizing the pelvis during stance-phase center-of-mass transfer — an example of drawing a line in the sand with explanation and evidence rather than authority alone (Module_6B_Part_B PDF pp.2–3). This is Weber's own account of a single case and does not establish a general diagnosis or treatment rule for similar presentations.

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this heuristic extends into interdisciplinary communication. [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the upstream problem this heuristic responds to.

He also introduces a leadership-honesty distinction: **technical leadership** (a leader with enough depth to personally teach the framework) versus **structural leadership** (a leader who instead ensures the right technical people are in place to do it); either is legitimate, but "technical coherence cannot be left to chance. Someone must own it" (p.2).

**When to apply** — Whenever the same concept has to be re-explained to different stakeholders more than once or twice in a season, treat that repetition itself as the signal to intervene, not just the individual instance to answer. Relevant to Baylor's own proposed intern curriculum, which already commits to sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3] — this heuristic argues those sessions exist specifically to eliminate a recurring translation cost, not just to build general awareness.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that some explanation will always be necessary, particularly concise executive-level updates for coaches; the goal is reducing unnecessary translation, not eliminating all of it (p.1). This heuristic also assumes the leader has honestly audited whether they personally have the technical depth to lead the education, or need to bring in someone who does (p.2); skipping that self-audit risks a leader attempting technical leadership they cannot actually deliver.

**Example** — Weber's pelvis/clam case: a rehabilitation issue had been framed narrowly as a strength problem (poor frontal-plane pelvis control treated with isolated abduction work), until technically grounded leadership reframed it as a motor-control problem, demonstrating the athletes were already strong enough in isolation and that the real issue was stabilizing the pelvis during stance-phase center-of-mass transfer — an example of drawing a line in the sand with explanation and evidence rather than authority alone (Module_6B_Part_B PDF pp.2–3). This is Weber's own account of a single case and does not establish a general diagnosis or treatment rule for similar presentations.

# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

**Why it works** — Naming a specific gap between each pair of stages turns a vague complaint ("the data doesn't seem to change anything") into a locatable failure point, the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] but applied at the level of a single decision's data pipeline rather than the department's overall structure.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). His expertise-gap point — "who sets and reviews the thresholds, including software defaults" — lands directly on a named gap in Baylor's own data dictionary, which is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS] — this framework gives that gap a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.

**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced — for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.

**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54) — the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.

# The Grey Zone: Naming Ownership Where Medical and Performance Overlap

**What it is** — Weber's term for the overlap between medical/physiotherapy staff and strength/performance staff, where differences in training, priorities, timelines, and risk tolerance become a problem specifically when the overlap has no agreed operating rules (Video Lab 6E summary, 00:00–02:44). His proposed governance: agree the phases, decision points, measures, and criteria the department will use; assign a named operational owner for each phase, define what that person can change independently, and state which decisions require escalation and who must be informed, and how quickly, when a plan changes (02:44–10:43). One example division he describes: medical leadership early in rehabilitation, strength staff taking operational responsibility for return-to-running, with both continuing to contribute — but he is explicit this division should shift when the actual skills and collaboration willingness of the specific practitioners warrant it, since "a job title alone does not establish who is best equipped for a specific task" (03:59–07:11).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is the same as the strategy/tactics model (see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]) applied to a specific high-stakes handoff: without a named owner per phase, both disciplines can reasonably believe the other is responsible, or both can independently act on the same decision point with different criteria. His team exercise makes the mismatch tangible: walk through one rehabilitation case twice, once from the physiotherapist's priorities and constraints and once from the strength coach's, then compare the two accounts at each handoff and agree ownership, progression criteria, information to transfer, change authority, and notification rules (10:43–13:02).

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play pathway where Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance/Athletics Performance both have a legitimate stake in the same phase. This is a direct structural answer to the exact gap named in Eric's own material: Applied Performance's role in return-to-performance is described as advisory, supplying information that supports Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. This framework's phase-by-phase ownership map is the concrete artifact that gap is missing.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's phase-division example (medical early, strength for return-to-running) is his own illustration, not a validated or universal division of labor; he states explicitly it should change based on who the actual practitioners are and how they work together, not be applied as a fixed template. This framework also does not resolve clinical criteria for a specific injury type — it governs who owns which decision, not what the decision's medical threshold should be.

**Example** — Weber's escalation rule: name an operational owner for each phase, state what that person can change independently, and specify which decisions must be escalated, plus who must be informed and how quickly when the athlete's plan changes (07:11–10:43).

**Related** — [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the general delegation model this framework applies to a specific handoff. [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the authority-gap failure mode this framework is built to prevent. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal criteria structure each phase's decision points would still need.

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — A system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system "as staff, technology, and knowledge change" treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup.

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. Pairs directly with Baylor's own stated annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4] — this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the "what could break this" question, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

**Why it works** — A system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system "as staff, technology, and knowledge change" treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup.

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. Pairs directly with Baylor's own stated annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4] — this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the "what could break this" question, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

14	# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise: have staff list five things that could derail the department, as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks (00:00–02:36).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is diagnostic, not just motivational: a CPD conversation reveals two different things at once — whether someone needs support to grow, and whether they are actually interested in progressing. That distinction maps directly onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): a staff member who has no CPD activity might be a knowledge gap, a motivation gap, or both, and the conversation is how a leader tells which.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. Fits naturally into Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own framing: "he proposes asking staff about continuing professional development and inviting brief presentations about recent learning" as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

12	---
13	
14	# Match Mentors to the Sport, Not Just the Discipline
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's stated preference, for performance-sport roles specifically, is to choose mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments," rather than mentors who share a technical discipline but not the sport context (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber does not give a mechanism beyond his own stated preference; the implicit reasoning is that comparable-sport experience carries tacit knowledge (competition calendar pressures, roster size, sport-specific injury patterns) that a mentor from an unrelated sport or setting would not have, even with equal or greater technical depth in the discipline itself.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a technically strong mentor from an unrelated sport and one with direct comparable-sport background. Directly relevant to Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] — this heuristic argues for weighting the football-specific voices in that mentoring structure, not just the general sport-science ones.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between sport-matched and discipline-matched mentors, and no guidance for cases where no sport-matched mentor is available. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for staff to "practice leadership before receiving the title" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.
27

2	type: library-entry
3	kind: framework
4	domain: performance-technology-and-leadership
5	book: old-bull-performance-course--old-bull
6	chapter: "Webinar 1 Part II"
7	topic: staff capability and engagement grid
8	category: [staff-development, leadership]
9	confidence: supported
10	ingest-tier: full-text
11	created: 2026-09-26
12	---
13	
14	# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix
15	
16	**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, not judgments of a person's worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is "does this person need more knowledge, more engagement, or both." Weber's advice to pick mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that it is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, "rather than a person's worth" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement "may limit a team's progress" (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.
27

# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise: have staff list five things that could derail the department, as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks (00:00–02:36).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is diagnostic, not just motivational: a CPD conversation reveals two different things at once — whether someone needs support to grow, and whether they are actually interested in progressing. That distinction maps directly onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): a staff member who has no CPD activity might be a knowledge gap, a motivation gap, or both, and the conversation is how a leader tells which.

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. Fits naturally into Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing: "he proposes asking staff about continuing professional development and inviting brief presentations about recent learning" as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

# Match Mentors to the Sport, Not Just the Discipline

**What it is** — Weber's stated preference, for performance-sport roles specifically, is to choose mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments," rather than mentors who share a technical discipline but not the sport context (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18).

**Why it works** — Weber does not give a mechanism beyond his own stated preference; the implicit reasoning is that comparable-sport experience carries tacit knowledge (competition calendar pressures, roster size, sport-specific injury patterns) that a mentor from an unrelated sport or setting would not have, even with equal or greater technical depth in the discipline itself.

**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a technically strong mentor from an unrelated sport and one with direct comparable-sport background. Directly relevant to Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] — this heuristic argues for weighting the football-specific voices in that mentoring structure, not just the general sport-science ones.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between sport-matched and discipline-matched mentors, and no guidance for cases where no sport-matched mentor is available. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.

**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for staff to "practice leadership before receiving the title" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, not judgments of a person's worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is "does this person need more knowledge, more engagement, or both." Weber's advice to pick mentors "who have worked in comparable sport settings and understand the demands of those environments" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that it is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, "rather than a person's worth" (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).

**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement "may limit a team's progress" (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick mentors with comparable sport-setting experience (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).

**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement "may limit a team's progress" (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use over roughly two decades (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber's implicit argument is that adopting a technology before an environment's procedures, staff skill, and interpretive norms have matured to match it recreates the tech-rich/procedure-poor problem he names in Lab 1C (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]): the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist.

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not "is this tool valid" but "has this tool, and my staff's ability to use it, matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost."

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and "maturity" here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption; earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline: "he contrasts early users of new tools with GPS, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use" (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

# Data to Information to Knowledge to Wisdom

**What it is** — Weber uses the standard data-information-knowledge-wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy to argue that storing measurements and building dashboards (data, information) does not, by itself, help a department make a decision (knowledge, wisdom); each step up the hierarchy requires additional interpretive work, not just more collection (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 03:27–04:42).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism connects directly to communication capacity: a coach or medical colleague handed a complex dashboard is left to do the interpretation themselves, which he illustrates with a "pick-up 52" analogy — see [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — meaning the recipient is handed a scattered deck and asked to reassemble it into an answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44).

**When to apply** — Reviewing any recurring report or dashboard against the question "does this hand the reader data, or does it hand them an answer." Useful as a design check on Baylor's own reporting: the Playbook's Development Plan already names "standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates" as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] — this hierarchy is a way to test a draft template before it ships (does it stop at data, or does it reach a stated recommendation).

**When NOT to apply** — The DIKW hierarchy is a widely used general communication model, not something original to Weber or specific to sport performance; he offers no sport-science-specific validation of it, only an application. It also does not specify how to move from one level to the next for a particular metric, only that the movement is necessary.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring caution: treating one favorable test result as a complete return-to-running answer is data or information, not knowledge, because it has not been checked against other convergent evidence (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] for the fuller version of this same caution.

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication practice this hierarchy motivates. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the evidentiary discipline needed to reach "knowledge." [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the practical bottleneck Weber ties to moving up this hierarchy.

**What it is** — Weber's "pick-up 52" analogy: handing a coach or medical colleague a complex, unfiltered dashboard is like scattering a deck of 52 cards on the floor and asking them to pick it up and make sense of it themselves (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44). His alternative: the communicator should begin with the recipient's actual question and decide which information is relevant to that question before presenting anything, specifying the equipment, standards, and reporting format up front (07:44–08:54).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is that a dashboard which "leaves the coach or medical colleague to do the interpretation" transfers cognitive work to the person least equipped to reconcile multiple measures against each other, and least likely to know which differences are within normal error. Framing the report around a stated question forces the practitioner, who has that context, to do the reconciliation once instead of the recipient doing it every time.

**When to apply** — Designing any recurring coach- or medical-facing report or dashboard, especially where Baylor's own gap analysis already flags standardized reporting templates as unbuilt [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. Also useful when a new coach or staff member joins and needs to be told what they will receive and why, matching the same communication checklist Lab 2C recommends for monitoring and testing (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a design heuristic for the recipient-facing layer of reporting; it does not argue against keeping a full, granular dataset available to the practitioners who need it. Weber gives no template for how to identify "the recipient's question" when it has not been stated, only that it should be established before building the report.

**Example** — Weber's own SpeedSig product classification, described as reducing many measures into a simpler signal while keeping detail available "for those who need it," is his illustration of the practice — offered as a product example, not independent evidence that the underlying classification is clinically or competitively valid (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 08:54–10:39).

14	# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — arguing this "reduce[s] ambiguity and give[s] both leaders and staff more room for focused work" (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure, which is what frees attention for harder problems.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is "worth the paperwork": onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing the credential-vault protocol his own gap analysis already flags as missing [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. It also gives a concrete rationale for the intern curriculum's stated goal of teaching "the how" alongside "the why" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1] — the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). A department whose SOPs are current can answer yes; Baylor's own Playbook shows the failure mode Weber warns against, since its NordBord section still documents a full roster-style collection protocol that was never updated after the practice was retired for football in 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8] — the procedure fell out of sync with the decision that had already been made.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.
27

12	---
13	
14	# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part III, staff should "begin with the athlete question or problem, then select a measurement tool" rather than starting from the equipment on hand (00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. Fits directly onto Baylor's Applied Performance data dictionary gap: the current dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. This principle gives that gap a specific fix order: name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.
27

13	
14	# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber pairs this with a statistical-interpretation point: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. Directly relevant to Baylor's own force-plate protocol: the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is exactly the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability — but Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test (the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues) [method-baseline.md Tensions #5], which is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.
21

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — Protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber pairs this with a statistical-interpretation point: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. Directly relevant to Baylor's own force-plate protocol: the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is exactly the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability — but Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test (the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues) [method-baseline.md Tensions #5], which is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run; a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19) — both symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.
