14	# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own outranks any device they might buy next: "it's the most powerful piece of performance tech you own," yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example: "I've been a strength and conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). A department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.
19	
20	**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. Reality-checks cleanly against Eric's own practice: he already reports running Python-adjacent workflows and building dashboards, and his gap analysis explicitly names "sport-specific data dictionaries" and "Baylor-specific technology workflows" as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3] — work that depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just the vendor tools.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code, only that the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).
25

13	
14	# Monitoring vs. Testing
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks cannot catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness — a real tension worth naming against Eric's own baseline, which states a preference for "weekly tracking... over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early" [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved — the two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his 12% RFD example and similar single-number illustrations are heuristics, not transferable thresholds; the actual analysis method appropriate for a given metric depends on the test and context (p.2, and see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.
27

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — arguing this "reduce[s] ambiguity and give[s] both leaders and staff more room for focused work" (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure, which is what frees attention for harder problems.

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is "worth the paperwork": onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing the credential-vault protocol his own gap analysis already flags as missing [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. It also gives a concrete rationale for the intern curriculum's stated goal of teaching "the how" alongside "the why" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1] — the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). A department whose SOPs are current can answer yes; Baylor's own Playbook shows the failure mode Weber warns against, since its NordBord section still documents a full roster-style collection protocol that was never updated after the practice was retired for football in 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8] — the procedure fell out of sync with the decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part III, staff should "begin with the athlete question or problem, then select a measurement tool" rather than starting from the equipment on hand (00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. Fits directly onto Baylor's Applied Performance data dictionary gap: the current dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. This principle gives that gap a specific fix order: name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# The Constraint on 2020s Practitioners Is Vetting Information, Not Finding More of It

**What it is** — Weber's historical framing, opening the course: sport science and strength-and-conditioning practice grew from Milo of Croton's progressive overload through research institutes, periodization theory, biomechanics, and increasing specialization, then accelerated further with GPS/inertial tracking, force measurement, online coaching content, academic reviews, and social media (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 00:00–09:06). His claim: for practitioners entering the field now, the binding constraint is "vetting, filtering, and integrating information," not finding more of it, in contrast to his own earlier reliance on academic sources and experienced coaches (09:06–11:41). He extends this to AI specifically: useful for preliminary research and helping a skilled coder work faster, but short AI summaries "can strip away nuance," and practitioners who lack the underlying skill may overtrust AI-generated code, training plans, or rehabilitation plans (same range).

**Why it works** — This is Weber's own historical narrative and personal contrast between "his day" and now, not a documented survey of practitioner information behavior; the mechanism (more channels producing more unfiltered volume) is plausible but not measured here.

**When to apply** — As a framing device when deciding how to train newer staff or interns: the emphasis shifts from "find more sources" toward "build a filter" — knowing which claims to trust, which social-media clips to discount, and which AI outputs need independent verification before use. Consistent with Eric's own course material's stated skepticism of "viral clip" training trends and its caution that a clip is "just a brief snapshot" stripped of context [method-baseline.md, Philosophy and decision principles].

**When NOT to apply** — Treat this as Weber's opinion and personal history, not as an evidenced claim about how practitioners as a group actually behave; the transcript is machine-generated and historical names/dates in this section should be checked against the audio before being repeated as fact (course README caveat). It should not be cited as a finding that AI tools are unreliable in general, only as Weber's specific caution about unverified AI-generated training or rehab content in the hands of someone without the underlying skill to check it.

**Example** — Weber's own closing framing for Part I: growth in technology and information has changed how performance departments operate, which he uses to set up the course's later modules on staff capability and decision structure (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 11:41–12:19).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the staff-capability framework this claim sets up. [[framework--rogers-adoption-curve-for-perf-tech]] — the companion framing for judging a specific technology's maturity.

# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own outranks any device they might buy next: "it's the most powerful piece of performance tech you own," yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example: "I've been a strength and conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). A department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. Reality-checks cleanly against Eric's own practice: he already reports running Python-adjacent workflows and building dashboards, and his gap analysis explicitly names "sport-specific data dictionaries" and "Baylor-specific technology workflows" as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3] — work that depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just the vendor tools.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code, only that the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.

**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.

# Monitoring vs. Testing

**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks cannot catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness — a real tension worth naming against Eric's own baseline, which states a preference for "weekly tracking... over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early" [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved — the two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his 12% RFD example and similar single-number illustrations are heuristics, not transferable thresholds; the actual analysis method appropriate for a given metric depends on the test and context (p.2, and see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].

**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.

15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow; forcing preparation and concise contributions works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone — aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Kaigi-transcript summary, 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that a decision meeting has different requirements from sharing information, creating solutions, or educating staff (00:00–02:18); using kaigi structure to force a decision before the options are actually narrowed to two or three, or before enough evidence exists, will produce a fast but poorly grounded call. His own Go/No-Go numbers (roughly 15–17 staff, under 30 seconds per player, 20-minute follow-up) are his example's parameters, not validated operating thresholds or a recommended clinical protocol.
23	
24	**When NOT to apply (continued)** — See [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for the broader set of meeting modes; kaigi is specifically the "decide" mode and should not be reached for when the actual need is "diagnose" or "build."
25	
26	**Example** — Weber's stalled-meeting rescue: when a broader problem-solving discussion stalls, explicitly announce the switch to decision mode, give it a fixed short window (his example: 10 minutes), and require a stated decision, an owner, and a documented outcome before the group moves on (12:14–13:23).
27

[[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this format sits inside. # The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from "what do we have" to "what does it produce and who acts on it." The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves.

**Why it works (strategy vs. tactics)** — Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to Baylor's own department model, where Applied Performance is explicitly a support/advisory role feeding decisions that Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine make [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of that shared workflow, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model].

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

[[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. # The Kaigi Decision Meeting

**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow; forcing preparation and concise contributions works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.

**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone — aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Kaigi-transcript summary, 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that a decision meeting has different requirements from sharing information, creating solutions, or educating staff (00:00–02:18); using kaigi structure to force a decision before the options are actually narrowed to two or three, or before enough evidence exists, will produce a fast but poorly grounded call. His own Go/No-Go numbers (roughly 15–17 staff, under 30 seconds per player, 20-minute follow-up) are his example's parameters, not validated operating thresholds or a recommended clinical protocol.

**When NOT to apply (continued)** — See [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for the broader set of meeting modes; kaigi is specifically the "decide" mode and should not be reached for when the actual need is "diagnose" or "build."

**Example** — Weber's stalled-meeting rescue: when a broader problem-solving discussion stalls, explicitly announce the switch to decision mode, give it a fixed short window (his example: 10 minutes), and require a stated decision, an owner, and a documented outcome before the group moves on (12:14–13:23).

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping this format requires. [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this format sits inside. # The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves.

**Why it works (strategy vs. tactics)** — Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to Baylor's own department model, where Applied Performance is explicitly a support/advisory role feeding decisions that Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine make [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of that shared workflow, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model].

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where the "decision" cell of this matrix gets formalized.

14	# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running "decide" structure on a "diagnose" problem, or vice versa). Fits directly onto Baylor's HHPR 5355 course structure and any Applied Performance staff meeting; the retrospective mode in particular gives a named structure to the kind of after-the-fact review Eric's own material shows happening informally around training decisions [method-baseline.md, Periodization and programming].
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs — that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda, and a leader using meetings to "gather perspectives that test their initial view before deciding" (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, which is a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's retrospective example: reviewing "a run of injuries" with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the fuller "decide" mode structure. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — a presentation format built for the "decide" mode specifically. [[heuristic--time-box-recurring-meetings]] — the time-discipline this typology assumes throughout.
27

13	
14	# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's practice for senior leaders: state a problem, then pause to hear staff views before offering an opinion, so the leader's own view does not anchor the discussion; he sometimes assigns someone to prepare an opposing case with evidence, and treats the resulting debate as a way to test his own assumptions before deciding (Lab 3D summary, 06:14–08:49). He restates the same practice in Podcast 6 with two named devices for structured dissent: the "tenth man" idea from *World War Z* (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation) and Edward de Bono's "six hats," used to deliberately examine a decision apart from the pressure around it and then from the athlete's or other stakeholders' point of view (Podcast 6 summary, 01:42–08:04). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure, and a leader who speaks first sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them. Formally assigning the dissenting role removes the social cost: the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.
19	
20	**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. Weber's own recurring calf-injury anecdote (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is his illustration of what happens when dissent has no formal channel and instead depends on finding the right messenger after the fact (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00).
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion; using it for every routine call would slow decision-making without adding much value. The film and historical references (World War Z, six hats) are illustrations of the practice, not evidence for its effectiveness in a performance department, and the calf-injury anecdote is a personal account that does not establish the training change's actual effect on injury rates.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own account: a coach who "listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail," rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--assign-meeting-ownership-to-develop-staff]] — the companion staff-development practice from the same lab. [[heuristic--review-the-system-on-a-schedule]] — the broader practice of scheduling this kind of challenge proactively rather than only after a problem appears.
27

**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. **When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion; using it for every routine call would slow decision-making without adding much value. **Example** — Weber's own account: a coach who "listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail," rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).

14	# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber treats running a meeting as a deliberate developmental exercise: giving a staff member ownership of a meeting's structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability builds confidence and practical leadership skill (Lab 3D summary, 00:46–02:25). His own example: assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist. Implementation notes: define the meeting's purpose, keep an agenda, hold time limits and agreed decision boundaries, and record an owner/action/due-date/review for each output, while giving the facilitator room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy (02:25–03:11; see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]). For less confident speakers, start small: one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time, and deliberately track who contributes so quieter staff are invited in with advance notice of when they will present (03:11–05:09).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is graduated exposure: a staff member who is given a bounded, low-stakes facilitation role (one slide, one topic) practices the mechanics of running structured discussion without the full weight of an open-ended meeting, then earns larger scope as competence shows. This mirrors the knowledge x behaviour matrix's developmental use (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): meeting ownership is a concrete vehicle for moving someone along the knowledge axis.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Identifying a staff member or intern ready for more responsibility, or building a structured on-ramp for a quieter staff member who has relevant expertise but does not volunteer it. Fits Baylor's proposed intern curriculum goal of a "professional portfolio of real work products" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — running an assigned meeting segment, with the agenda and decision log as artifacts, is one such work product.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for judging when a staff member is ready to move from a one-slide, one-topic assignment to a full meeting; that judgment is left to the assigning leader. This heuristic also assumes the leader is willing to accept the facilitation being less polished at first than if the leader ran it themselves — it is a deliberate trade of short-term efficiency for staff development.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's advancement path: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot; increase responsibility from there (03:11–05:09).
25

# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill

# The Decision Log: Action, Owner, Due Date, Review

**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format: the meeting-typology "decide" mode requires "an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review" (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with "one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point, recorded in the decision log" (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with "the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update" (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down "creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed" (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). Without a record, a verbal decision is subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). Directly usable as a template for Baylor's own return-to-play and technology-adoption decisions, where Eric's own gap analysis already notes that no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol exists in writing [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — a decision log does not supply the criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale — Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

**Example** — Weber's stoplight-storytelling version adds one more requirement to the same four fields: "every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date" (Lab 3C summary, 05:51–06:23) — closing the loophole of an ambiguous "wait and see" outcome with no owner attached.

**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — where this log format originates in the course. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the more detailed version of "next step" for higher-stakes decisions. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — the presentation format that ends with this same log.

Without a record, a verbal decision is subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). Directly usable as a template for Baylor's own return-to-play and technology-adoption decisions, where Eric's own gap analysis already notes that no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol exists in writing [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — a decision log does not supply the criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale — Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

**Example** — Weber's stoplight-storytelling version adds one more requirement to the same four fields: "every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date" (Lab 3C summary, 05:51–06:23) — closing the loophole of an ambiguous "wait and see" outcome with no owner attached.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running "decide" structure on a "diagnose" problem, or vice versa). Fits directly onto Baylor's HHPR 5355 course structure and any Applied Performance staff meeting; the retrospective mode in particular gives a named structure to the kind of after-the-fact review Eric's own material shows happening informally around training decisions [method-baseline.md, Periodization and programming].

It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs — that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda, and a leader using meetings to "gather perspectives that test their initial view before deciding" (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, which is a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.

# Assign Someone to Argue the Other Side Before You Decide

**What it is** — Weber's practice for senior leaders: state a problem, then pause to hear staff views before offering an opinion, so the leader's own view does not anchor the discussion; he sometimes assigns someone to prepare an opposing case with evidence, and treats the resulting debate as a way to test his own assumptions before deciding (Lab 3D summary, 06:14–08:49). He restates the same practice in Podcast 6 with two named devices for structured dissent: the "tenth man" idea from *World War Z* (assign someone to formally argue against the group's favored explanation) and Edward de Bono's "six hats," used to deliberately examine a decision apart from the pressure around it and then from the athlete's or other stakeholders' point of view (Podcast 6 summary, 01:42–08:04). He also describes a coach who listened quietly before asking specifically where a plan might fail (04:59–06:34).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism is that a team sharing one process can still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure, and a leader who speaks first sets an anchor that makes dissent socially costly for everyone after them. Formally assigning the dissenting role removes the social cost: the person arguing against the plan is doing their job, not breaking rank.

**When to apply** — High-stakes or hard-to-reverse decisions, especially ones the group has converged on quickly or that fit a familiar pattern the department has not recently questioned. Weber's own recurring calf-injury anecdote (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is his illustration of what happens when dissent has no formal channel and instead depends on finding the right messenger after the fact (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for which decisions warrant an assigned dissenter versus ordinary discussion; using it for every routine call would slow decision-making without adding much value. The film and historical references (World War Z, six hats) are illustrations of the practice, not evidence for its effectiveness in a performance department, and the calf-injury anecdote is a personal account that does not establish the training change's actual effect on injury rates.

**Example** — Weber's own account: a coach who "listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail," rather than stating a view first and then asking for objections to it (04:59–06:34).

**Related** — [[heuristic--assign-meeting-ownership-to-develop-staff]] — the companion staff-development practice from the same lab. [[heuristic--review-the-system-on-a-schedule]] — the broader practice of scheduling this kind of challenge proactively rather than only after a problem appears.

14	# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Naming a specific gap between each pair of stages turns a vague complaint ("the data doesn't seem to change anything") into a locatable failure point, the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] but applied at the level of a single decision's data pipeline rather than the department's overall structure.

# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

14	# The Grey Zone: Naming Ownership Where Medical and Performance Overlap
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's term for the overlap between medical/physiotherapy staff and strength/performance staff, where differences in training, priorities, timelines, and risk tolerance become a problem specifically when the overlap has no agreed operating rules (Video Lab 6E summary, 00:00–02:44). 17

23	
24	**Example** — Weber's escalation rule: name an operational owner for each phase, state what that person can change independently, and specify which decisions must be escalated, plus who must be informed and how quickly when the athlete's plan changes (07:11–10:43).

13	
14	# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gap** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence, which he frames as a shared responsibility ("practitioners share responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information"); **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's core claim is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). Naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that "good work isn't landing" into a specific, auditable question: which of the five links actually failed.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1) — a useful test to run against Baylor's own KPI-threshold principle, which is named as a departmental operating principle but has no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol documented anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play].
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's authority-gap distinction: overriding a technical recommendation is "sometimes necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gap is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.
27

13	
14	# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision: does staff have "enough independent, relevant information to act" (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is "one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance" (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism, illustrated with two anecdotes (a soccer knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL history, and a hamstring return-to-play case), is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Combining them and updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive (Podcast 2 summary, 02:20–17:35).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). Gives a concrete practice for a tension in Eric's own material: the course transcripts argue "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3] — evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach; they do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury or that any specific stack of tests can clear an athlete to play, and medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions outside this framework's scope (Podcast 2 summary, 18:15 caveat). It also does not specify how many independent streams are "enough" for a given decision — that judgment is left to the practitioner.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the single-measurement discipline this framework scales up. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where a completed evidence stack feeds a formal go/hold/stop decision. [[principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]] — the reliability discipline each stream in the stack still needs individually.
27

13	
14	# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.
17	
18	**Why it works** — A system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system "as staff, technology, and knowledge change" treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup.
19	
20	**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. Pairs directly with Baylor's own stated annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4] — this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the "what could break this" question, not only an update-the-document pass.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — A system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system "as staff, technology, and knowledge change" treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup.

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. Pairs directly with Baylor's own stated annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4] — this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the "what could break this" question, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

**Why it works** — Naming a specific gap between each pair of stages turns a vague complaint ("the data doesn't seem to change anything") into a locatable failure point, the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] but applied at the level of a single decision's data pipeline rather than the department's overall structure.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). His expertise-gap point — "who sets and reviews the thresholds, including software defaults" — lands directly on a named gap in Baylor's own data dictionary, which is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS] — this framework gives that gap a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.

**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced — for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.

**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54) — the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.
