# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise: have staff list five things that could derail the department, as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks (00:00–02:36).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is diagnostic, not just motivational: a CPD conversation reveals two different things at once — whether someone needs support to grow, and whether they are actually interested in progressing. That distinction maps directly onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): a staff member who has no CPD activity might be a knowledge gap, a motivation gap, or both, and the conversation is how a leader tells which.

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. Fits naturally into Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing, per the lesson summary: asking staff about CPD and inviting a short presentation on something recently learned, as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

# Match Mentors to the Sport, Not Just the Discipline

**What it is** — Weber's stated preference, for performance-sport roles specifically, is to choose mentors with direct experience in comparable sport settings who understand the demands of those environments, rather than mentors who share a technical discipline but not the sport context (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18).

**Why it works** — Weber does not give a mechanism beyond his own stated preference; the implicit reasoning is that comparable-sport experience carries tacit knowledge (competition calendar pressures, roster size, sport-specific injury patterns) that a mentor from an unrelated sport or setting would not have, even with equal or greater technical depth in the discipline itself.

**When to apply** — Assigning a mentor to a new hire, intern, or staff member being developed toward more responsibility, when there is a real choice between a technically strong mentor from an unrelated sport and one with direct comparable-sport background. Directly relevant to Baylor's proposed intern curriculum, which is explicitly adapting a Clemson Olympic-sports model "to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5] — this heuristic argues for weighting the football-specific voices in that mentoring structure, not just the general sport-science ones.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Weber's stated opinion, not a tested claim; he gives no comparison of outcomes between sport-matched and discipline-matched mentors, and no guidance for cases where no sport-matched mentor is available. In that case the choice is between an imperfect option and no mentor at all, which this heuristic does not address.

**Example** — Weber's framing places this immediately after his call for aspiring leaders to start practicing leadership before they hold the title (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 02:36–03:59), positioning mentor selection as part of a deliberate leadership-development pipeline rather than an incidental pairing.

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] — the companion practice for identifying who needs a mentor. [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this selection criterion sits inside.

# Data to Information to Knowledge to Wisdom

**What it is** — Weber uses the standard data-information-knowledge-wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy to argue that storing measurements and building dashboards (data, information) does not, by itself, help a department make a decision (knowledge, wisdom); each step up the hierarchy requires additional interpretive work, not just more collection (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 03:27–04:42).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism connects directly to communication capacity: a coach or medical colleague handed a complex dashboard is left to do the interpretation themselves, which the lesson summary describes with a pick-up-52 analogy — see [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the recipient is handed a scattered deck and asked to reassemble it into an answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44).

**When to apply** — Reviewing any recurring report or dashboard against the question of whether it hands the reader raw data or hands them an answer they can act on. Useful as a design check on Baylor's own reporting: the Playbook's Development Plan already names "standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates" as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] — this hierarchy is a way to test a draft template before it ships (does it stop at data, or does it reach a stated recommendation).

**When NOT to apply** — The DIKW hierarchy is a widely used general communication model, not something original to Weber or specific to sport performance; he offers no sport-science-specific validation of it, only an application. It also does not specify how to move from one level to the next for a particular metric, only that the movement is necessary.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring caution: treating one favorable test result as a complete return-to-running answer is data or information, not knowledge, because it has not been checked against other convergent evidence (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] for the fuller version of this same caution.

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication practice this hierarchy motivates. # Start From the Recipient's Question, Not the Full Dashboard ("Pick-Up 52")

**What it is** — Weber's pick-up-52 analogy, per the lesson summary: handing a coach or medical colleague a complex, unfiltered dashboard is like scattering a deck of 52 cards on the floor and asking them to pick it up and make sense of it themselves (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44). His alternative: the communicator should begin with the recipient's actual question and decide which information is relevant to that question before presenting anything, specifying the equipment, standards, and reporting format up front (07:44–08:54).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is that a dashboard that leaves the coach or medical colleague to do the interpretation themselves transfers cognitive work to the person least equipped to reconcile multiple measures against each other, and least likely to know which differences are within normal error. Framing the report around a stated question forces the practitioner, who has that context, to do the reconciliation once instead of the recipient doing it every time.

**When to apply** — Designing any recurring coach- or medical-facing report or dashboard, especially where Baylor's own gap analysis already flags standardized reporting templates as unbuilt [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. Also useful when a new coach or staff member joins and needs to be told what they will receive and why, matching the same communication checklist Lab 2C recommends for monitoring and testing (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a design heuristic for the recipient-facing layer of reporting; it does not argue against keeping a full, granular dataset available to the practitioners who need it. Weber gives no template for how to identify the recipient's actual question when it has not been stated, only that it should be established before building the report.

**Example** — Weber's own SpeedSig product classification, described as reducing many measures into a simpler signal while keeping detail available for those who need it, is his illustration of the practice, offered as a product example, not independent evidence that the underlying classification is clinically or competitively valid (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 08:54–10:39).

**Related** — [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — the model this heuristic operationalizes. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parallel communication checklist for monitoring and testing reports.

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure, which is what frees attention for harder problems.

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is "worth the paperwork": onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing the credential-vault protocol his own gap analysis already flags as missing [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]. It also gives a concrete rationale for the intern curriculum's stated goal of teaching "the how" alongside "the why" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1] — the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). A department whose SOPs are current can answer yes; Baylor's own Playbook shows the failure mode Weber warns against, since its NordBord section still documents a full roster-style collection protocol that was never updated after the practice was retired for football in 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8] — the procedure fell out of sync with the decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. Fits directly onto Baylor's Applied Performance data dictionary gap: the current dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. This principle gives that gap a specific fix order: name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — Protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber pairs this with a statistical-interpretation point: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. Directly relevant to Baylor's own force-plate protocol: the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is exactly the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability — but Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test (the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues) [method-baseline.md Tensions #5], which is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run; a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19) — both symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the companion discipline against reacting to a single result. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where "what triggers action" gets formally defined.

# The Constraint on 2020s Practitioners Is Vetting Information, Not Finding More of It

**What it is** — Weber's historical framing, opening the course: sport science and strength-and-conditioning practice grew from Milo of Croton's progressive overload through research institutes, periodization theory, biomechanics, and increasing specialization, then accelerated further with GPS/inertial tracking, force measurement, online coaching content, academic reviews, and social media (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 00:00–09:06). His claim: for practitioners entering the field now, the binding constraint is vetting, filtering, and integrating information, not finding more of it, in contrast to his own earlier reliance on academic sources and experienced coaches (09:06–11:41). He extends this to AI specifically: useful for preliminary research and helping a skilled coder work faster, but short AI summaries can strip away nuance, and practitioners who lack the underlying skill may overtrust AI-generated code, training plans, or rehabilitation plans (same range).

**Why it works** — This is Weber's own historical narrative and personal contrast between his early career and now, not a documented survey of practitioner information behavior; the mechanism (more channels producing more unfiltered volume) is plausible but not measured here.

**When to apply** — As a framing device when deciding how to train newer staff or interns: the emphasis shifts from finding more sources toward building a filter, knowing which claims to trust, which social-media clips to discount, and which AI outputs need independent verification before use. Consistent with Eric's own course material's stated skepticism of "viral clip" training trends and its caution that a clip is "just a brief snapshot" stripped of context [method-baseline.md, Philosophy and decision principles].

**When NOT to apply** — Treat this as Weber's opinion and personal history, not as an evidenced claim about how practitioners as a group actually behave; the transcript is machine-generated and historical names/dates in this section should be checked against the audio before being repeated as fact (course README caveat). It should not be cited as a finding that AI tools are unreliable in general, only as Weber's specific caution about unverified AI-generated training or rehab content in the hands of someone without the underlying skill to check it.

**Example** — Weber's own closing framing for Part I: growth in technology and information has changed how performance departments operate, which he uses to set up the course's later modules on staff capability and decision structure (Webinar 1 Part I summary, 11:41–12:19).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the staff-capability framework this claim sets up. [[framework--rogers-adoption-curve-for-perf-tech]] — the companion framing for judging a specific technology's maturity.

# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own outranks any device they might buy next: "it's the most powerful piece of performance tech you own," yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example, per the transcript (which renders "strength and conditioning" as "straight conditioning," an evident ASR error): "I've been a [strength and] conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). A department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. # Monitoring vs. Testing

**What it is** — Weber's separation of two questions that are often mashed together. **Monitoring** answers "has something changed right now," sits on a days-to-weeks horizon, and is "status and trend": day-to-day jump performance, session exposure/tolerance, readiness markers, short-term fatigue signals, feeding load adjustments, recovery decisions, and progression/regression calls (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1). **Testing** answers "have we improved capacity across a training phase," sits on a weeks-to-months horizon, and is "progress": pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two, evaluating whether the program is working (p.1). His explicit warning: short-term monitoring methods (rolling averages, exponentially weighted moving averages) are built to detect drift from a recent baseline, not to answer whether capacity improved across a training phase — "different questions require different analysis" (p.1–2). His communication checklist for either one: state what is being evaluated, why, how often, what output the coach will receive, and what different results would trigger, before pressure to act arrives (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that a rolling baseline moves with the athlete, so it can hide a slow, real change in capacity even while flagging every short-term dip; conversely, comparing two widely separated phase blocks cannot catch a same-week acute status change. Using the wrong analysis method for the question produces a plausible-looking number that answers a different question than the one being asked.

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness — a real tension worth naming against Eric's own baseline, which states a preference for "weekly tracking... over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early" [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved — the two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit, in the companion Lab 2E material, that his 12% RFD example and similar single-number illustrations are heuristics, not transferable thresholds; the actual analysis method appropriate for a given metric depends on the test and context (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.2, and see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). This framework also does not resolve which specific quality to monitor or test for a given sport — that is the prior question in [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]].

**Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**Related** — [[heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift]] — the specific failure mode this framework warns against. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for the "if this, then that" decision matrix Weber describes here. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the shared "name the quality first" operating principle.

# The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves. The same audit embeds a delegation model: Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to Baylor's own department model, where Applied Performance is explicitly a support/advisory role feeding decisions that Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine make [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of that shared workflow, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model].

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where the "decision" cell of this matrix gets formalized.

# The Decision Log: Action, Owner, Due Date, Review

**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format, per the lesson summaries: the meeting-typology **decide** mode requires an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale, per the lesson summary, is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). Without a record, a verbal decision is subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). Directly usable as a template for Baylor's own return-to-play and technology-adoption decisions, where Eric's own gap analysis already notes that no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol exists in writing [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — a decision log does not supply the criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale — Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

# Name the Meeting Mode Before You Set the Agenda: Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build

**What it is** — Weber's four meeting modes, each with a different structure and expected output. **Decide**: a clear question with limited options, using pre-reading, time-boxed input, an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review — the same structure as the kaigi format (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14; see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]). **Diagnose**: a known problem whose cause or solution is uncertain, gathering perspectives and hypotheses on a defined problem with time-boxed contributions (Weber's example: roughly 30 minutes), assigning a smaller group to gather more information if unresolved, then scheduling a later decision (02:14–04:03). **Inform**: sharing updates and context, with an explicit warning that inform meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving if not held to that purpose (04:37–05:02). **Build**: co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week, giving people room to contribute, considering psychological safety, and allowing time to digest ideas across possibly several meetings rather than forcing one immediate decision (05:34–06:18). Weber also names two composite formats: an **operations meeting** (brief status updates, blocker removal, ownership assignment, combining informing with quick decisions, 05:02–05:34) and a **retrospective/after-action review** (a factual, blameless timeline of what happened, using measures and named gaps, translated into procedure changes, 06:18–07:08). His practical rule: for each agenda item, write one verb — decide, diagnose, inform, or build — plus the question, expected output, time limit, and pre-reading (07:08–08:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: naming the mode in advance tells participants what kind of contribution is needed and protects creative or diagnostic work from being cut short by premature decision pressure, while letting genuinely decidable questions move fast once the options are known. A single staff meeting can move through several modes in sequence, provided each segment states its own purpose and output so participants know which mode they are in at any given moment (04:03–04:37).

**When to apply** — Building or reviewing any recurring departmental meeting's agenda, or diagnosing why a specific meeting series feels unproductive (often because it is running **decide** structure on a **diagnose** problem, or vice versa). Fits directly onto Baylor's HHPR 5355 course structure and any Applied Performance staff meeting; the retrospective mode in particular gives a named structure to the kind of after-the-fact review Eric's own material shows happening informally around training decisions [method-baseline.md, Periodization and programming].

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no evidence that naming a mode improves meeting outcomes beyond his own stated experience; this is a proposed practice, not a tested intervention. It also does not resolve who decides which mode an agenda item needs; that judgment is left to whoever sets the agenda. A leader who uses a meeting to gather perspectives that test their own initial view before deciding (07:08–08:09) is deliberately using diagnose-mode dynamics inside what will eventually become a decide-mode outcome, a legitimate but easily-missed hybrid use.

**Example** — Weber's retrospective example, per the lesson summary: reviewing a run of injuries with a factual timeline and named missing information, kept blameless, then translated into a procedure change rather than a verdict on any individual (06:18–07:08).

**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the fuller **decide**-mode structure. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — a presentation format built for the **decide** mode specifically. [[heuristic--time-box-recurring-meetings]] — the time-discipline this typology assumes throughout.

# Give Staff Ownership of a Meeting to Build Their Leadership Skill

**What it is** — Weber treats running a meeting as a deliberate developmental exercise: giving a staff member ownership of a meeting's structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability builds confidence and practical leadership skill (Lab 3D summary, 00:46–02:25). His own example: assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist. Implementation notes: define the meeting's purpose, keep an agenda, hold time limits and agreed decision boundaries, and record an owner/action/due-date/review for each output, while giving the facilitator room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy (02:25–03:11; see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]). For less confident speakers, start small: one slide, one topic, a short time slot, then increase responsibility over time, and deliberately track who contributes so quieter staff are invited in with advance notice of when they will present (03:11–05:09).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is graduated exposure: a staff member who is given a bounded, low-stakes facilitation role (one slide, one topic) practices the mechanics of running structured discussion without the full weight of an open-ended meeting, then earns larger scope as competence shows. This mirrors the knowledge x behaviour matrix's developmental use (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): meeting ownership is a concrete vehicle for moving someone along the knowledge axis.

**When to apply** — Identifying a staff member or intern ready for more responsibility, or building a structured on-ramp for a quieter staff member who has relevant expertise but does not volunteer it. Fits Baylor's proposed intern curriculum goal of a "professional portfolio of real work products" [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4] — running an assigned meeting segment, with the agenda and decision log as artifacts, is one such work product.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for judging when a staff member is ready to move from a one-slide, one-topic assignment to a full meeting; that judgment is left to the assigning leader. This heuristic also assumes the leader is willing to accept the facilitation being less polished at first than if the leader ran it themselves — it is a deliberate trade of short-term efficiency for staff development.

**Example** — Weber's advancement path: start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, a short time slot; increase responsibility from there (03:11–05:09).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the broader developmental framework this practice serves. [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the companion senior-leadership practice from the same lab.

# The Decision Pathway: Six Stages, Five Gaps to Audit

**What it is** — Weber's model of the full route from an observation to an action: **data capture -> quality control -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication -> decision and action** (Video Lab 6D summary, 00:00–02:02). He names a specific gap between each pair of adjacent stages. **(1) Dirty data** (capture to quality control): check that the collection protocol was actually followed and that anomalies are caught before entering reports or a long-term database, with a named owner for the check. **(2) Expertise** (quality control to analysis): a reliable measurement can still be judged against an unsuitable threshold, or without its normal context, including software defaults that were never reviewed. **(3) Interpretation** (analysis to meaning): a number can reach a meeting with no one stating what it means for the athlete or the decision, and excess data can exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. **(4) Communication** (interpretation to decision-maker): technical language can obscure the actual requested action; Weber recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. **(5) Authority** (recommendation to action): even a clear recommendation can be ignored without a formal decision gate or override process; he calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions (02:02–10:50).

**Why it works** — Naming a specific gap between each pair of stages turns a vague complaint ("the data doesn't seem to change anything") into a locatable failure point, the same diagnostic logic as [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] but applied at the level of a single decision's data pipeline rather than the department's overall structure.

**When to apply** — Weber's own stated practical use: trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it (10:52–12:11). His expertise-gap point, that someone needs to set and review the thresholds a measurement is judged against, including software defaults, lands directly on a named gap in Baylor's own data dictionary, which is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, with no sport-specific or position-specific thresholds currently documented [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment; Load monitoring and GPS] — this framework gives that gap a specific owner-and-process fix rather than leaving it as a general observation.

**When NOT to apply** — This framework audits the pipeline's structure; it does not itself validate whether a given threshold or software default is the right one, only that someone should be reviewing it. It also assumes a decision pathway already exists to be traced — for a genuinely new signal with no established pathway, the encoding and integration frameworks (see [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]]) are the prior step.

**Example** — Weber's communication-gap framing: leading with a clear recommendation first, and putting supporting technical detail in a form the recipient can actually use, rather than requiring the recipient to extract the recommendation from technical language themselves (05:32–08:54) — the same discipline as [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] applied specifically at the decision-pathway's communication stage.

**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the department-level companion to this pipeline-level audit. [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication-gap discipline this framework names as stage four. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal structure for stage five's authority and action.

# The Grey Zone: Naming Ownership Where Medical and Performance Overlap

**What it is** — Weber's term for the overlap between medical/physiotherapy staff and strength/performance staff, where differences in training, priorities, timelines, and risk tolerance become a problem specifically when the overlap has no agreed operating rules (Video Lab 6E summary, 00:00–02:44). His proposed governance: agree the phases, decision points, measures, and criteria the department will use; assign a named operational owner for each phase, define what that person can change independently, and state which decisions require escalation and who must be informed, and how quickly, when a plan changes (02:44–10:43). One example division he describes: medical leadership early in rehabilitation, strength staff taking operational responsibility for return-to-running, with both continuing to contribute — but he is explicit this division should shift when the actual skills and collaboration willingness of the specific practitioners warrant it, since "a job title alone does not establish who is best equipped for a specific task" (03:59–07:11).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is the same as the strategy/tactics model (see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]]) applied to a specific high-stakes handoff: without a named owner per phase, both disciplines can reasonably believe the other is responsible, or both can independently act on the same decision point with different criteria. His team exercise makes the mismatch tangible: walk through one rehabilitation case twice, once from the physiotherapist's priorities and constraints and once from the strength coach's, then compare the two accounts at each handoff and agree ownership, progression criteria, information to transfer, change authority, and notification rules (10:43–13:02).

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play pathway where Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance/Athletics Performance both have a legitimate stake in the same phase. This is a direct structural answer to the exact gap named in Eric's own material: Applied Performance's role in return-to-performance is described as advisory, supplying information that supports Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. This framework's phase-by-phase ownership map is the concrete artifact that gap is missing.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's phase-division example (medical early, strength for return-to-running) is his own illustration, not a validated or universal division of labor; he states explicitly it should change based on who the actual practitioners are and how they work together, not be applied as a fixed template. This framework also does not resolve clinical criteria for a specific injury type — it governs who owns which decision, not what the decision's medical threshold should be.

**Example** — Weber's escalation rule: name an operational owner for each phase, state what that person can change independently, and specify which decisions must be escalated, plus who must be informed and how quickly when the athlete's plan changes (07:11–10:43).

**Related** — [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the general delegation model this framework applies to a specific handoff. [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the authority-gap failure mode this framework is built to prevent. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the formal criteria structure each phase's decision points would still need.

# The Integration Problem: Five Break Points Between Data and Decision

**What it is** — Weber's framework for a specific failure mode: a practitioner collects genuinely useful information, but it never influences a decision because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. "Good information does not guarantee influence... this is usually not a knowledge problem" (The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf p.1). His five break points, tracing a signal from collection to action: **(1) language gap** — teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation; **(2) decision pathway gap** — no agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, or what triggers a conversation; **(3) authority gap** — a senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation (Weber favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision, rather than a silent override); **(4) relationship deficit** — the person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence, which he frames as a shared responsibility ("practitioners share responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information"); **(5) process absence** — missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments (Video Lab 6A summary, 06:58–13:14; cheat sheet p.1). His diagnostic test: "if your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (cheat sheet p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's core claim is that departments fail through structure, not intent: recommendations get ignored, diluted, or misunderstood because the environment lacks the pathway to handle them, not because the underlying analysis was wrong (cheat sheet p.1). Naming five distinct break points turns a vague sense that "good work isn't landing" into a specific, auditable question: which of the five links actually failed.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a past decision where technically sound information did not change the outcome, or auditing a department's current pathway for a specific recurring signal (e.g., a fatigue flag, an asymmetry finding). Weber's own audit question directly names the exercise: "you need to ask whether your data has ever directly changed a major decision, and whether you can trace the path from collection to action" (cheat sheet p.1) — a useful test to run against Baylor's own KPI-threshold principle, which is named as a departmental operating principle but has no specific RTP criteria or phased-return protocol documented anywhere in the reviewed corpus [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play].

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own account of a past bone-stress-injury case, where he says he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use, is a personal anecdote illustrating the communication point; it does not establish a general injury-prediction rule from training surface, and the transcript cannot verify the causal claim (Video Lab 6A summary, 13:14–15:38). This framework also assumes the underlying information was sound in the first place; it diagnoses pathway failure, not measurement or inference failure (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] for that separate question).

**Example** — Weber's authority-gap distinction: overriding a technical recommendation is "sometimes necessary, but it should happen transparently and with explanation" (cheat sheet p.1) — the failure mode is the silent override, not the override itself.

**Related** — [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the next-stage problem (same information, different disciplinary lens) that this framework's language gap connects to. [[framework--decision-pathway-six-stages-five-gaps]] — a parallel, more granular breakdown of the data-to-decision pipeline. [[framework--grey-zone-overlap-ownership]] — where the authority gap is resolved for medical/performance overlap specifically.

# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision: does staff have "enough independent, relevant information to act" (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is "one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance" (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism, illustrated with two anecdotes (a soccer knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL history, and a hamstring return-to-play case), is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Combining them and updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive (Podcast 2 summary, 02:20–17:35).

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). Gives a concrete practice for a tension in Eric's own material: the course transcripts argue "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3] — evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that his anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach; they do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury or that any specific stack of tests can clear an athlete to play, and medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions outside this framework's scope (Podcast 2 summary, 18:15 caveat). It also does not specify how many independent streams are "enough" for a given decision — that judgment is left to the practitioner.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.

**Related** — [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the single-measurement discipline this framework scales up. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where a completed evidence stack feeds a formal go/hold/stop decision. [[principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]] — the reliability discipline each stream in the stack still needs individually.

# Schedule Time to Ask What Could Break the System, Before It Does

**What it is** — Weber's closing recommendation in Podcast 6: leaders should set aside regular time outside daily operations specifically to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system, rather than waiting for a failure to force the review (Podcast 6 summary, 00:00–01:41, 11:13–13:58). His stated reasoning: a team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure (03:22–04:06) — the same blind spot his structured-dissent practices (see [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]]) are meant to catch inside a specific meeting, applied here as a standing habit rather than a one-off intervention.

**Why it works** — A system that is currently working provides no natural trigger to question it; problems tend to surface only after something has already gone wrong. Scheduling the review removes the dependency on a failure event, and revising the system "as staff, technology, and knowledge change" treats department process as something that ages and needs periodic maintenance, not a one-time setup.

**When to apply** — At a natural cadence point (end of season, start of a new training block, after staff turnover, or when a new technology is adopted), independent of whether anything has visibly gone wrong. Pairs directly with Baylor's own stated annual Playbook review cycle each May [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4] — this heuristic argues that review should explicitly include the "what could break this" question, not only an update-the-document pass.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's own illustration (a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team that only changed course once a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept) is a personal anecdote about decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' actual cause or the training change's effect, and should not be read as evidence for a specific calf-injury intervention (Podcast 6 summary, 08:04–10:00). This heuristic also gives no specific cadence or format for the review — only that it should happen on a schedule rather than only reactively.

**Example** — Weber's own framing of the practice: identify what could go wrong in an apparently stable system, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change (11:13–13:58).

**Related** — [[heuristic--structured-dissent-before-deciding]] — the in-meeting version of the same challenge-your-own-plan discipline. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the broader case for documented, periodically reviewed procedure.

14	# CM2: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum
15	
16	**What it is** — A four-stage shared map Weber uses to describe where an athlete sits in a program, so staff across strength and conditioning, rehab, and sports science can communicate quickly without re-litigating vocabulary. The stages: **Control** (single-joint, isolated activation, used early in rehab or with an athlete who cannot yet sequence joints), **Movement** (multi-joint, integrated patterns that are "viable and repeatable... without falling apart"), **Capacity** (building the "engine": volume and tolerance for work, where "a lot of athletes live for large parts of the year"), and **Maximum** (short exposures to peak speed, force, or power once capacity is built) (Lab 1A transcript, 00:06:05–00:08:32). Athletes move forward when ready and back to an earlier stage when needed. Weber names it twice in the same recording, once as "CM2" (00:06:10) and once as "STM squared" (00:09:21); the automated transcript may have mis-heard one or both labels, so neither name should be treated as verified without checking the audio.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is coordination, not physiology: a large staff (athlete, performance manager, several S&C coaches, athletic trainers, physios, sports science staff) needs "a very, very simple language... to allow people to move quickly and not get bogged down" (00:08:32–00:09:00). Placing an athlete on the map ("he's not moving that well, we need to drop him back to control") gives a leader a one-line status update across disciplines without needing agreement on deeper theory.
19	
20	**When to apply** — As a discussion shorthand in interdisciplinary handoffs (rehab to performance, performance to sport coach) when the question is "where is this athlete in the process" rather than a specific numeric threshold. Maps loosely onto the Vermeil hierarchy already used in Eric's own course material (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) [method-baseline.md, Strength and power], so it could sit alongside rather than replace that existing shared vocabulary.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber presents this as one example teams can adapt, not a validated developmental model ("I made my [CM2] thing up. You don't have to use that," 00:09:26–00:09:31). It carries no criteria for how to know an athlete has met a stage's bar, no timelines, and no evidence it improves outcomes; it is a communication convention, not an assessment protocol. Do not substitute it for Baylor's own testing/reassessment criteria [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment].
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's illustration: an athlete in early rehab who cannot yet sequence multiple joints stays in single-joint Control work (e.g., isolated clam exercises) rather than progressing to complex movement drills; once that control is established, the priority becomes "getting moving" as fast as safely possible rather than lingering in isolated work (00:07:07–00:07:44).
25	
26	**Related** — [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the ordering rule this map is built to support.
27

14	# The Tech Stack Reality Check
15	
16	**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that most performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department "chases noise and calls it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). Directly usable against Baylor's own documented gap: current GPS/VALD workflow SOPs are described by Eric's own gap analysis as "generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail" outside the Catapult workflow [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2] — this audit's Step 1–3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" and his contrast with himself ("I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models... that's me because I want to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the companion audit that adds who-does-what-with-it. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics behind Step 2. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the chain this audit sets up (procedure to reliability to confidence to defensible decisions).
27

13	
14	# Measurement vs. Inference
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples: calling a lower countermovement-jump result "neurological fatigue," or a GPS change "tissue stress" — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Collapsing the distinction lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. Applies directly to Baylor's mRSI-as-readiness-marker practice: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen objective readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example: what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). # Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples: calling a lower countermovement-jump result "neurological fatigue," or a GPS change "tissue stress" — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Collapsing the distinction lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. Applies directly to Baylor's mRSI-as-readiness-marker practice: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen objective readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example: what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02) — the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

14	# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. This is a direct, stated gap in Eric's own corpus: mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], but no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus — Weber's framework would treat that as the non-negotiable missing step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that "you don't need to become a statistician here" but the minimum thinking is still required (p.1); this framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. His "greater than MDC / greater than SWC" examples are heuristics, not universal calculation rules — the appropriate method depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary, 02:27–03:53).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's rate-of-force-development (RFD) case: a 12% difference may be uninformative if it falls within the metric's own local measurement variability, because execution consistency, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences create large swings in calculated RFD; see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response (pp.2–3). The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] — the specific fix for a noisy metric like RFD. # CM2: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum

**What it is** — A four-stage shared map Weber uses to describe where an athlete sits in a program, so staff across strength and conditioning, rehab, and sports science can communicate quickly without re-litigating vocabulary. The stages: **Control** (single-joint, isolated activation, used early in rehab or with an athlete who cannot yet sequence joints), **Movement** (multi-joint, integrated patterns that are "viable and repeatable... without falling apart"), **Capacity** (building the "engine": volume and tolerance for work, where "a lot of athletes live for large parts of the year"), and **Maximum** (short exposures to peak speed, force, or power once capacity is built) (Lab 1A transcript, 00:06:05–00:08:32). Athletes move forward when ready and back to an earlier stage when needed. Weber names it twice in the same recording, once as "CM2" (00:06:10) and once as "STM squared" (00:09:21); the automated transcript may have mis-heard one or both labels, so neither name should be treated as verified without checking the audio.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is coordination, not physiology: a large staff (athlete, performance manager, several S&C coaches, athletic trainers, physios, sports science staff) needs "a very, very simple language... to allow people to move quickly and not get bogged down" (00:08:32–00:09:00). Placing an athlete on the map ("he's not moving that well, we need to drop him back to control") gives a leader a one-line status update across disciplines without needing agreement on deeper theory.

**When to apply** — As a discussion shorthand in interdisciplinary handoffs (rehab to performance, performance to sport coach) when the question is "where is this athlete in the process" rather than a specific numeric threshold. Maps loosely onto the Vermeil hierarchy already used in Eric's own course material (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) [method-baseline.md, Strength and power], so it could sit alongside rather than replace that existing shared vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber presents this as one example teams can adapt, not a validated developmental model ("I made my [CM2] thing up. You don't have to use that," 00:09:26–00:09:31). It carries no criteria for how to know an athlete has met a stage's bar, no timelines, and no evidence it improves outcomes; it is a communication convention, not an assessment protocol. Do not substitute it for Baylor's own testing/reassessment criteria [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment].

**Example** — Weber's illustration: an athlete in early rehab who cannot yet sequence multiple joints stays in single-joint Control work (e.g., isolated clam exercises) rather than progressing to complex movement drills; once that control is established, the priority becomes "getting moving" as fast as safely possible rather than lingering in isolated work (00:07:07–00:07:44).

**Related** — [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the ordering rule this map is built to support.
