# The Tech Stack Reality Check

**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that most performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department "chases noise and calls it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.

**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). Directly usable against Baylor's own documented gap: current GPS/VALD workflow SOPs are described by Eric's own gap analysis as "generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail" outside the Catapult workflow [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2] — this audit's Step 1–3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.

**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" and his contrast with himself ("I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models... that's me because I want to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the companion audit that adds who-does-what-with-it. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics behind Step 2. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the chain this audit sets up (procedure to reliability to confidence to defensible decisions).

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples: calling a lower countermovement-jump result "neurological fatigue," or a GPS change "tissue stress" — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — Collapsing the distinction lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. Applies directly to Baylor's mRSI-as-readiness-marker practice: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen objective readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example: what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02) — the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# Strategy Is the Highway, Tactics Are Changing Lanes

**What it is** — Weber's delegation model: **strategy** is the department's direction, standards, and the key questions it cares about, described as "the highway"; **tactics** are the day-to-day choices staff make within that direction (which tool to deploy, how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure, how to respond to what they see), described as "changing lanes" (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1–2). The stated goal is to give staff tactical freedom while the leader maintains strategic alignment (p.2). He restates the same model in Webinar 3 Part III as a direct delegation rule: the leader names the destination and boundaries, staff choose tactics within them, with more discretion given to an experienced colleague than a new hire, and explicit criteria for which decisions must be escalated (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is that without a named boundary, staff either wait for permission on every tactical choice (killing responsiveness) or drift from department standards one small decision at a time (killing alignment). Naming the highway once, in writing, removes the need to re-negotiate it for every individual tactical call.

**When to apply** — Structuring how much autonomy a staff member has over test selection, session adjustments, or reporting choices, especially as a department scales past a size where informal alignment happens naturally. Gives a concrete vocabulary for Eric's own department-model gap: the Playbook's stated peer-department framing for Applied Performance is not fully reconciled with the "support staff" framing that appears elsewhere in the same corpus [method-baseline.md Tensions #2] — naming the specific highway (standards, questions Applied Performance owns) versus the lanes (tactical choices left to individual practitioners) is a direct way to resolve that ambiguity in practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no method for determining where the highway's boundaries should sit for a given department or decision type; that judgment call is left entirely to the leader. It is also not a substitute for the formal escalation criteria a decision gate provides (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) when the stakes are high enough to need a documented pass/fail/borderline threshold rather than a general delegation boundary.

**Example** — Weber's contrast: an experienced colleague gets wider tactical discretion than a new hire under the same strategic direction, with explicit agreement on which decisions must be escalated rather than decided independently (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 03:56–06:30).

**Related** — [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the audit this delegation model is embedded in. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the more formal structure for higher-stakes decisions. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the companion communication rules from the same Webinar 3 material.

# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC

**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. This is a direct, stated gap in Eric's own corpus: mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], but no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus — Weber's framework would treat that as the non-negotiable missing step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that "you don't need to become a statistician here" but the minimum thinking is still required (p.1); this framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. His "greater than MDC / greater than SWC" examples are heuristics, not universal calculation rules — the appropriate method depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary, 02:27–03:53).

**Example** — Weber's rate-of-force-development (RFD) case: a 12% difference may be uninformative if it falls within the metric's own local measurement variability, because execution consistency, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences create large swings in calculated RFD; see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response (pp.2–3). The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.

**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] — the specific fix for a noisy metric like RFD. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — where reliability is first introduced as a step-2 check.

14	# When a Metric Is Noisy, Widen the Threshold, Tighten the Protocol, or Pick a Different Metric
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's three-option response when a metric shows high inherent variability, illustrated with rate of force development (RFD): "the takeaway is not 'never use RFD.' The takeaway is: when a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose a more stable metric for decision gates" (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.2). He attributes RFD's typical noise to three sources: execution-consistency demands, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences that produce large swings in the calculated value (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — This gives a leader three genuinely different levers instead of one binary (use it or drop it): widening the decision threshold accepts the noise and raises the bar for calling a change real; tightening the protocol (standardizing onset detection, warm-up, instructions) reduces the noise itself; switching metrics sidesteps the problem by choosing a more stable measure of a similar underlying quality. Which lever is right depends on whether the noise comes from the measurement process (fixable by protocol) or is closer to genuine biological/mechanical variability (better handled by a wider threshold or a different metric).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time a metric is flagged as unreliable during the reliability-vs-sensitivity audit (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]), rather than either dropping the metric outright or continuing to use it with an unexamined threshold. Directly applicable to any force-plate "fluffy" metric in Baylor's own reporting framework (peak power, average power, RFD), which the adopted Hawkin Dynamics ODSF metric-selection framework already flags as needing "a specific, defensible rationale" before inclusion [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this heuristic is the concrete follow-up once a metric like RFD is found to be noisy in-house.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not say how to choose between the three levers for a given case, only that one of them is the right response to noise; this is a decision menu, not a decision rule. It also does not apply to a metric whose problem is not noise but validity (measuring the wrong construct entirely) — that is a different failure mode, addressed by [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]].
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's stated leadership framing for this whole statistical package: "if staff are using tests with unknown reliability, then when they bring you a number, there is no foundation for trust. Statistical rigour gives you credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, decision gates that work" (p.2).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the diagnostic this heuristic responds to. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit's own procedure-first fix for a different but related problem (undocumented protocol).
27

13	
14	# A Rolling Baseline Can Hide the Exact Long-Term Drift You Are Trying to Catch
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" — because the reference point (the rolling average itself) moves along with the slow change you would need to detect (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — A rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over eight weeks, a 7- or 14-day rolling average tracks that drift and never flags it as a deviation, because the "baseline" itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question ("has this athlete's capacity actually improved this block"). This is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and Eric's stated preference for weekly tracking to catch plateaus.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.
27

14	# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision
15	
16	**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("first clinical review within X hours," "imaging expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). Agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. Names a specific structure for a gap Eric's own department documentation already states as a principle without specifying the mechanics: "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as an operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. This framework also assumes a genuine, pre-identifiable decision point exists; it is not suited to open-ended diagnostic or brainstorming work (see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" is the wrong mode to reach for).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — where the "if this result, then this action" decision matrix first appears. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping companion to a gate's decision.
27

13	
14	# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).
17	
18	**Why it works** — This is the coach-facing application of the recipient-question discipline in [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: a report in unfamiliar technical vocabulary forces the coach to translate it before they can use it, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary translation cost Weber later names explicitly as a leadership failure mode (see [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]]). Agreeing shared verbal categories once removes that translation step from every future report.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. Directly relevant to Baylor's own stated gap: standardized coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] — this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around, which may take a full season to establish for a new coach.
23

# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement

**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).

**Why it works** — This is the coach-facing application of the recipient-question discipline in [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: a report in unfamiliar technical vocabulary forces the coach to translate it before they can use it, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary translation cost Weber later names explicitly as a leadership failure mode (see [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]]). Agreeing shared verbal categories once removes that translation step from every future report.

**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. Directly relevant to Baylor's own stated gap: standardized coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] — this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around, which may take a full season to establish for a new coach.

**Example** — Weber's specific practice: verbal running categories, agreed once with the coach, used consistently in reporting instead of raw speed-band units (01:09–06:11).

# When a Metric Is Noisy, Widen the Threshold, Tighten the Protocol, or Pick a Different Metric

**What it is** — Weber's three-option response when a metric shows high inherent variability, illustrated with rate of force development (RFD): "the takeaway is not 'never use RFD.' The takeaway is: when a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose a more stable metric for decision gates" (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.2). He attributes RFD's typical noise to three sources: execution-consistency demands, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences that produce large swings in the calculated value (p.2).

**Why it works** — This gives a leader three genuinely different levers instead of one binary (use it or drop it): widening the decision threshold accepts the noise and raises the bar for calling a change real; tightening the protocol (standardizing onset detection, warm-up, instructions) reduces the noise itself; switching metrics sidesteps the problem by choosing a more stable measure of a similar underlying quality. Which lever is right depends on whether the noise comes from the measurement process (fixable by protocol) or is closer to genuine biological/mechanical variability (better handled by a wider threshold or a different metric).

**When to apply** — Any time a metric is flagged as unreliable during the reliability-vs-sensitivity audit (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]), rather than either dropping the metric outright or continuing to use it with an unexamined threshold. Directly applicable to any force-plate "fluffy" metric in Baylor's own reporting framework (peak power, average power, RFD), which the adopted Hawkin Dynamics ODSF metric-selection framework already flags as needing "a specific, defensible rationale" before inclusion [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring] — this heuristic is the concrete follow-up once a metric like RFD is found to be noisy in-house.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not say how to choose between the three levers for a given case, only that one of them is the right response to noise; this is a decision menu, not a decision rule. It also does not apply to a metric whose problem is not noise but validity (measuring the wrong construct entirely) — that is a different failure mode, addressed by [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]].

**Example** — Weber's stated leadership framing for this whole statistical package: "if staff are using tests with unknown reliability, then when they bring you a number, there is no foundation for trust. Statistical rigour gives you credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, decision gates that work" (p.2).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the diagnostic this heuristic responds to. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit's own procedure-first fix for a different but related problem (undocumented protocol).

# A Rolling Baseline Can Hide the Exact Long-Term Drift You Are Trying to Catch

**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" — because the reference point (the rolling average itself) moves along with the slow change you would need to detect (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).

**Why it works** — A rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over eight weeks, a 7- or 14-day rolling average tracks that drift and never flags it as a deviation, because the "baseline" itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change.

**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question ("has this athlete's capacity actually improved this block"). This is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and Eric's stated preference for weekly tracking to catch plateaus.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.

**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.

# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision

**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("first clinical review within X hours," "imaging expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). Agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.

**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. Names a specific structure for a gap Eric's own department documentation already states as a principle without specifying the mechanics: "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as an operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.

**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. This framework also assumes a genuine, pre-identifiable decision point exists; it is not suited to open-ended diagnostic or brainstorming work (see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" is the wrong mode to reach for).

**Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — where the "if this result, then this action" decision matrix first appears. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping companion to a gate's decision.

# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement

**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).

**Why it works** — This is the coach-facing application of the recipient-question discipline in [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: a report in unfamiliar technical vocabulary forces the coach to translate it before they can use it, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary translation cost Weber later names explicitly as a leadership failure mode (see [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]]). Agreeing shared verbal categories once removes that translation step from every future report.

**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. Directly relevant to Baylor's own stated gap: standardized coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2] — this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around, which may take a full season to establish for a new coach.

**Example** — Weber's specific practice: verbal running categories, agreed once with the coach, used consistently in reporting instead of raw speed-band units (01:09–06:11).

# Agree Which Channel Carries What, and When, Before the Pressure Arrives

**What it is** — Weber's set of communication rules meant to be settled in advance rather than negotiated in the moment: specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected on it; for injuries specifically, state in advance when the coach receives a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may follow; agree the timing and form of post-training reports, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats; mark messages by urgency or purpose; and make meeting invitations state their objective, length, and required preparation, with project assignments stating the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult, plus expected response times (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 06:11–10:09). In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism ties directly to attention management: predictable communication and clear roles reduce the time a leader spends interpreting routine requests, freeing that attention for planning and harder problems (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 00:00–00:59, 02:52–05:05). His example: a head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about "training load" from entirely different concerns and technical backgrounds, so the leader needs pre-agreed shared language and channel norms to respond efficiently rather than re-deriving the right answer for each asker every time (00:59–02:46).

**When to apply** — Setting up communication norms for a new season, a new coach relationship, or a newly formed interdisciplinary group, particularly around injury updates, where ambiguity about timing is most costly. Gives concrete structure to Eric's own department's stated advisory role: Applied Performance's job is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play] — this heuristic is the channel-and-timing layer that makes that advisory information actually arrive when it is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are presented as his own management practice, not independently validated outcomes (Webinar 3 Part II summary caveat). This is also not a substitute for the decision-gate timeframes in [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]], which cover the higher-stakes case of formal go/hold/stop decisions rather than routine reporting cadence.

**Example** — Weber's military-analogy caution in Part I: he explicitly warns that military and sport stakes differ, using the analogy only to illustrate that rehearsed communication routines let a team act without inventing a process under pressure — in one AFL case, coach and performance staff changed a session live during play because they shared enough technical language to estimate consequences for specific players in real time (Webinar 3 Part I summary, 05:05–09:03).

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this set of rules extends. [[heuristic--translate-metrics-into-coaches-vocabulary]] — the vocabulary-specific version of this same discipline. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation-boundary companion from the same Webinar.

14	# The Encoding Problem: Same Athlete, Different Lens
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's observation that different professional groups reviewing the same athlete and the same data routinely see different problems, not because they disagree about the facts, but because those facts are "encoded" differently by discipline: a physiotherapist sees tissue tolerance, healing, and rehabilitation progress; a medical practitioner sees health status and risk; a strength and conditioning coach sees readiness, output, and return-to-performance demands; a sports scientist sees load, exposure, and the numerical pathway to competition; a coach sees availability (can the athlete train, can the athlete play) (Module_6B_Part_A PDF p.1). His proposed fix is a written, shared case framework: document how a given scenario (his example: a hamstring injury) will be assessed, the checkpoints, expected timing, and who acts at each handoff, built collaboratively with medical, physiotherapy, strength, and sport science staff so each group also learns what the others do (Video Lab 6B summary, 02:44–06:37; PDF p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism: when staff understand what other disciplines are doing, "departments become less defensive, less territorial, and more collaborative... staff are more willing to share information, raise concerns early, and adjust without fear or confusion" (PDF p.1). He is explicit this is not about eliminating disciplinary difference — healthy technical disagreement should be "respected and examined" — but about ensuring differences operate inside a shared structure rather than each discipline silently running its own model (PDF p.2).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any interdisciplinary case (injury, load management, return-to-play) where different departments have historically produced different read-outs of the same athlete without a documented shared plan. Directly names the coordination Baylor's own department model already implies but does not fully specify in writing: Applied Performance's stated role is to enable Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions [method-baseline.md, Department model], and this framework is a concrete method (a written pathway, checkpoints, and criteria per case type) for making that enabling role operational rather than aspirational.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber distinguishes healthy technical challenge from a staff member working outside the agreed process; the framework is meant to protect the former and surface the latter, not to suppress disagreement (PDF p.2). His own anecdote — presenting injury-risk evidence that was new and unfamiliar to a coach and doctor who lacked a shared framework for understanding it, followed by the predicted injuries occurring — is a personal account illustrating a communication failure, not evidence that the specific injury-risk claim itself was correct (PDF p.2).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own summary of the stakes: "correct data is not enough. If the leader cannot get the information understood across disciplines, the work has failed at the level that matters most" (PDF p.2).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--integration-problem-five-break-points]] — the upstream framework this problem sits inside (specifically the language gap). [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]] — the direct follow-on once an encoding gap has been identified. 13	
14	# Constant Translation Is a Diagnostic Signal: Replace It With Education
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's argument that repeatedly explaining the same concept to different stakeholders (medical, physiotherapy, strength and conditioning, sports science, coaching) is not just a communication cost but a symptom that the environment has not been educated to a common operating understanding (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1). He calls this a genuine "cognitive cost" and "performance leak inside the organisation," since it drains time and attention that could go to higher-level problems (p.1). His prescribed response: avoid translation where possible and replace it with education, treating a recurring need to re-explain the same idea as useful diagnostic information rather than an inconvenience to absorb (p.1). He offers two implementation routes depending on context: drawing a firm, clearly stated line in how the system will operate (faster, more likely to create friction, appropriate when confusion is already embedded), or building alignment through workshops, internal CPD, and structured educational sessions (slower, better suited where there is more time or openness) (p.1).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism ties this directly to the discipline-equals-freedom chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed... that frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (p.1). He also introduces a leadership-honesty distinction: **technical leadership** (a leader with enough depth to personally teach the framework) versus **structural leadership** (a leader who instead ensures the right technical people are in place to do it); either is legitimate, but "technical coherence cannot be left to chance. Someone must own it" (p.2).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Whenever the same concept has to be re-explained to different stakeholders more than once or twice in a season, treat that repetition itself as the signal to intervene, not just the individual instance to answer. Relevant to Baylor's own proposed intern curriculum, which already commits to sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3] — this heuristic argues those sessions exist specifically to eliminate a recurring translation cost, not just to build general awareness.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that some explanation will always be necessary, particularly concise executive-level updates for coaches; the goal is reducing unnecessary translation, not eliminating all of it (p.1). This heuristic also assumes the leader has honestly audited whether they personally have the technical depth to lead the education, or need to bring in someone who does (p.2); skipping that self-audit risks a leader attempting technical leadership they cannot actually deliver.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's pelvis/clam case: a rehabilitation issue had been framed narrowly as a strength problem (poor frontal-plane pelvis control treated with isolated abduction work), until technically grounded leadership reframed it as a motor-control problem, demonstrating the athletes were already strong enough in isolation and that the real issue was stabilizing the pelvis during stance-phase center-of-mass transfer — an example of drawing a line in the sand with explanation and evidence rather than authority alone (Module_6B_Part_B PDF pp.2–3). This is Weber's own account of a single case and does not establish a general diagnosis or treatment rule for similar presentations.
25	
26	**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this heuristic extends into interdisciplinary communication. [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the upstream problem this heuristic responds to.
27

# Constant Translation Is a Diagnostic Signal: Replace It With Education

**What it is** — Weber's argument that repeatedly explaining the same concept to different stakeholders (medical, physiotherapy, strength and conditioning, sports science, coaching) is not just a communication cost but a symptom that the environment has not been educated to a common operating understanding (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1). He calls this a genuine "cognitive cost" and "performance leak inside the organisation," since it drains time and attention that could go to higher-level problems (p.1). His prescribed response: avoid translation where possible and replace it with education, treating a recurring need to re-explain the same idea as useful diagnostic information rather than an inconvenience to absorb (p.1). He offers two implementation routes depending on context: drawing a firm, clearly stated line in how the system will operate (faster, more likely to create friction, appropriate when confusion is already embedded), or building alignment through workshops, internal CPD, and structured educational sessions (slower, better suited where there is more time or openness) (p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism ties this directly to the discipline-equals-freedom chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed... that frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (p.1). He also introduces a leadership-honesty distinction: **technical leadership** (a leader with enough depth to personally teach the framework) versus **structural leadership** (a leader who instead ensures the right technical people are in place to do it); either is legitimate, but "technical coherence cannot be left to chance. Someone must own it" (p.2).

**When to apply** — Whenever the same concept has to be re-explained to different stakeholders more than once or twice in a season, treat that repetition itself as the signal to intervene, not just the individual instance to answer. Relevant to Baylor's own proposed intern curriculum, which already commits to sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3] — this heuristic argues those sessions exist specifically to eliminate a recurring translation cost, not just to build general awareness.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that some explanation will always be necessary, particularly concise executive-level updates for coaches; the goal is reducing unnecessary translation, not eliminating all of it (p.1). This heuristic also assumes the leader has honestly audited whether they personally have the technical depth to lead the education, or need to bring in someone who does (p.2); skipping that self-audit risks a leader attempting technical leadership they cannot actually deliver.

**Example** — Weber's pelvis/clam case: a rehabilitation issue had been framed narrowly as a strength problem (poor frontal-plane pelvis control treated with isolated abduction work), until technically grounded leadership reframed it as a motor-control problem, demonstrating the athletes were already strong enough in isolation and that the real issue was stabilizing the pelvis during stance-phase center-of-mass transfer — an example of drawing a line in the sand with explanation and evidence rather than authority alone (Module_6B_Part_B PDF pp.2–3). This is Weber's own account of a single case and does not establish a general diagnosis or treatment rule for similar presentations.

**Related** — [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the underlying chain this heuristic extends into interdisciplinary communication. [[framework--encoding-problem-shared-case-framework]] — the upstream problem this heuristic responds to.

14	# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.
27

14	# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC
15	
16	**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], and no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus. **Inference:** Weber's framework would treat that missing figure as the non-negotiable step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that "you don't need to become a statistician here" but the minimum thinking is still required (p.1); this framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. His "greater than MDC / greater than SWC" examples are heuristics, not universal calculation rules — the appropriate method depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary, 02:27–03:53).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's rate-of-force-development (RFD) case: a 12% difference may be uninformative if it falls within the metric's own local measurement variability, because execution consistency, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences create large swings in calculated RFD; see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response (pp.2–3). The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] — the specific fix for a noisy metric like RFD. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — where reliability is first introduced as a step-2 check.
27

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], and no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus. **Inference:** Weber's framework would treat that missing figure as the non-negotiable step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.

14	# The Tech Stack Reality Check
15	
16	**What it is** — A three-step audit for an existing department, done before buying anything new. Step 1: inventory what you have **as measurement systems, not brands** ("people say 'we're doing NordBord.' NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength," Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). Weber's named categories: your computer (spreadsheets vs. real analysis/dashboard/coding capability), wearables (GNSS/GPS + IMU, not just "GPS"), force plates (force over time, not "jump height machines"), force transducers/load cells (isometrics, Nordics, dynamometry, where "if your setup changes, your test changes"), and linear position transducers (GymAware/FLEX-style, which need standardized naming, setup, ROM rules, and reporting rules) (pp.1–3). Step 2: for each measurement, establish **reliability** — can you repeat the number within a known error band, both within-session and between-session (p.3; Lab 1C transcript 00:03:47–00:04:45). Step 3: write down the **procedure** (warm-up, familiarization, instructions, trial structure) for at least one tool, because "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures... a procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:04:45–00:05:02; PDF p.3).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's argument is that most performance environments are "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (PDF p.1), which produces noise and decisions that feel like guesswork. Confusing a brand for the underlying test hides what is actually being measured; skipping reliability means a department "chases noise and calls it insight" (PDF p.3) the first time two measurements disagree.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Before adding new technology, and as a standing onboarding document for new staff ("if you started a job this week... you need to be able to set standards for your staff to follow," Lab 1C transcript 00:05:07–00:05:29). **Eric's baseline:** documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting), except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]. **Inference:** this audit's Step 1-3 sequence is a concrete way to close that gap tool by tool.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a starting-point audit, not a statistics course; it names ICC/typical-error-style reliability concepts only in passing (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the fuller treatment). It also assumes a department already owns the technology being audited; it is not a tool-selection or purchasing framework, and it takes no position on which tools are worth owning in the first place.
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own admission that most practitioners "treat their laptop like a typewriter" and his contrast with himself ("I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models... that's me because I want to push myself further up the chain") illustrates the audit's first, most-overlooked category: the computer itself as a performance tool (Lab 1C transcript 00:01:13–00:02:32; see [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]]).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the specific claim about computer/coding skill this audit surfaces. [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]] — the companion audit that adds who-does-what-with-it. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics behind Step 2. [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]] — the chain this audit sets up (procedure to reliability to confidence to defensible decisions).
27

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. He calls means-versus-modality "an old thing... an old Russian coaching concept," not his own invention. The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# System Reliability vs. Individual Sensitivity: ICC, SEM, MDC, and SWC

**What it is** — Weber separates two questions that a decision gate's criteria depend on. **System-level reliability** ("can we trust the test at all") covers the whole system, not just the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, athlete execution. Its tools: **ICC** (intraclass correlation coefficient, how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials — relative reliability), **SEM/TE** (standard error of measurement / typical error, the size of the noise in real units — absolute reliability), and **MDC95** (minimal detectable change, how much change is needed to be confident a shift exceeds typical noise at high confidence) (Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf p.1). **Individual-level monitoring sensitivity** ("can we detect meaningful change in this athlete") uses within-athlete typical error or coefficient of variation (CV%) to define **SWC** (smallest worthwhile change: the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real) (p.1). His key distinction: "MDC answers: is it beyond noise? SWC answers: is it worth caring about?" — both matter, and they serve different purposes (p.1). His combined decision logic: change below MDC95 is likely noise; above MDC95, likely real; above SWC, likely meaningful; above both, act with confidence; real but not meaningful, note and watch without overreacting (p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's argument: "technology doesn't become valuable because it measures something. It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with confidence: is this change real, or is it noise?" (p.1). Without an MDC/SWC ladder, every observed change looks equally actionable, and a decision gate's pass/fail/borderline criteria (see [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]) have no defensible basis.

**When to apply** — Setting or reviewing the numeric threshold behind any decision gate, and specifically before trusting a daily readiness metric enough to act on small day-to-day changes in it. **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the department's chosen readiness marker, described as "objective, consistent, and actionable" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], and no MDC95, SWC, or typical-error figure for mRSI appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus. **Inference:** Weber's framework would treat that missing figure as the non-negotiable step before any single-day mRSI change is used to make a training-load call.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that "you don't need to become a statistician here" but the minimum thinking is still required (p.1); this framework does not supply Baylor-specific ICC/SEM/MDC/SWC values for any test, only the structure for deriving and using them. His "greater than MDC / greater than SWC" examples are heuristics, not universal calculation rules — the appropriate method depends on the test and context (Lab 2E summary, 02:27–03:53).

**Example** — Weber's rate-of-force-development (RFD) case: a 12% difference may be uninformative if it falls within the metric's own local measurement variability, because execution consistency, onset-detection choices, and small timing differences create large swings in calculated RFD; see [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] for his recommended response (pp.2–3). The 12% figure is his anecdotal example, not a transferable threshold.

**Related** — [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the gate structure this statistics package supports. [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] — the specific fix for a noisy metric like RFD. [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — where reliability is first introduced as a step-2 check.

# Tighten One Recurring Meeting to Protect Staff Capacity

**What it is** — Weber's "20 minutes of discipline" structure for recurring operational decision meetings: send information roughly 24 hours in advance so attendees can read and consider it, state the required outcome at the start, keep discussion to what is working, what is not, and what needs to change, name who decides when a decision is needed, close with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update, start and stop on time (a visible timer where useful), and route useful off-topic items to a "parking lot" with an owner and next step (Podcast 3 summary, 07:20–11:11). "20 minutes" is his target for suitable routine meetings, not a limit he applies to every discussion (00:00–01:28). His challenge to the listener is to tighten just **one** recurring meeting, then ask whether anything valuable was lost and whether its outputs improved (12:16–16:44).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale is capacity protection: time saved in a tightened recurring meeting is time preserved for analysis, project work, and the training/treatment schedule itself (00:00–01:28, 02:58–04:24). Pre-reading and a stated required outcome shift the meeting's actual work (absorbing context, forming an initial view) to before the room convenes, so the meeting itself is spent on discussion and decision rather than briefing.

**When to apply** — Any standing weekly or daily operational meeting that has grown past its original purpose (a status update that has become a discussion, a discussion that has become a debate). Weber's own examples of what a tightened format looks like: a planning meeting using short timed rounds to collect responses to three questions from five people (about 40 minutes, described as preparing months of work), and short daily stand-ups surfacing completed work, next work, and blockers (01:28–02:58, 11:11–11:26).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber explicitly distinguishes this format from brainstorming and relationship-building, and recommends preparation, smaller pieces, and small multidisciplinary groups for genuinely complex problems rather than forcing them into a tight recurring slot (12:16–15:31); see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" mode is the wrong fit. His efficiency claims (the 40-minute planning meeting "prepared months of work") are his own account, not measured against an alternative.

**Example** — Weber's own operational rule for the parking lot: an off-topic issue that is nonetheless useful gets a named owner and a next step, so it is captured without derailing the meeting's actual agenda (10:08–11:11).

**Related** — [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this time-discipline applies within. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the closing record this format shares with the course's other meeting formats.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use over roughly two decades (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber's implicit argument is that adopting a technology before an environment's procedures, staff skill, and interpretive norms have matured to match it recreates the tech-rich/procedure-poor problem he names in Lab 1C (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]): the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist.

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not whether the tool is valid in principle, but whether the tool, and the staff's ability to use it, have matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and the maturity claim here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption; earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline, per the lesson summary: he contrasts early adopters of new tools with GPS specifically, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use over roughly two decades (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.
