# Report in the Coach's Existing Words, Without Losing the Link to the Measurement

**What it is** — Weber's recommendation: replace technical language with terms the audience already uses, while keeping the connection back to the underlying measurement intact. His AFL example: he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units (Webinar 3 Part II summary, 01:09–06:11). He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning a given coach's preferred words and report format early in the season, since different coaches want very different amounts and formats of information (07:48–08:39).

**Why it works** — This is the coach-facing application of the recipient-question discipline in [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]]: a report in unfamiliar technical vocabulary forces the coach to translate it before they can use it, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary translation cost Weber later names explicitly as a leadership failure mode (see [[heuristic--replace-translation-with-early-education]]). Agreeing shared verbal categories once removes that translation step from every future report.

**When to apply** — Building or revising any coach-facing report template, and specifically at the start of a season or with a new coach, before habits and expectations have set. **Eric's baseline:** standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. **Inference:** this heuristic argues the template design process should start with the coach's own vocabulary, established early, rather than a generic vendor-report format.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber does not argue for dropping technical precision internally among performance and medical staff, only for translating it at the coach-facing layer; the underlying measurement and its documented reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) should not be diluted, only re-expressed. It also assumes a coach's preferred vocabulary is knowable and stable enough to build a template around, which may take a full season to establish for a new coach.

**Example** — Weber's specific practice: verbal running categories, agreed once with the coach, used consistently in reporting instead of raw speed-band units (01:09–06:11).

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the general communication principle this applies to coaches specifically. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the companion rules for when and how coach-facing information is delivered.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber's implicit argument is that adopting a technology before an environment's procedures, staff skill, and interpretive norms have matured to match it recreates the tech-rich/procedure-poor problem he names in Lab 1C (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]): the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist.

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not whether the tool is valid in principle, but whether the tool, and the staff's ability to use it, have matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and the maturity claim here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption; earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline, per the lesson summary: he contrasts early adopters of new tools with GPS specifically, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

# Ask Staff About Their CPD to Surface Both Support Needs and Ambition

**What it is** — Weber's suggested practice: ask staff directly about their continuing professional development (CPD) and invite brief presentations about something they recently learned (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21). He pairs this with a related opening exercise: have staff list five things that could derail the department, as a way to get people examining their own contribution and the team's bottlenecks (00:00–02:36).

**Why it works** — Weber's reasoning is diagnostic, not just motivational: a CPD conversation reveals two different things at once — whether someone needs support to grow, and whether they are actually interested in progressing. That distinction maps directly onto the knowledge x behaviour matrix's two axes (see [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]): a staff member who has no CPD activity might be a knowledge gap, a motivation gap, or both, and the conversation is how a leader tells which.

**When to apply** — Regular staff check-ins, annual development conversations, or when trying to figure out who on staff is ready for more responsibility versus who needs a defined training plan. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's proposed intern curriculum already states interns should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products," not just device-operation checklists [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.4]. **Inference:** a CPD check-in is a low-cost way to track whether that portfolio is actually forming.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no structure for how often to ask, what to do with the answer, or how to handle a staff member who cannot name any recent CPD; this is a prompt, not a full performance-management process. It also should not be the sole input into a personnel decision (see the caution in [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]]).

**Example** — Weber's own framing, per the lesson summary: asking staff about CPD and inviting a short presentation on something recently learned, as a low-friction way to open the conversation (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 04:18–05:21).

**Related** — [[framework--knowledge-behaviour-matrix]] — the grid this practice is meant to inform. [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the companion practice for staff who need external development support.

14	# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix
15	
16	**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick mentors with comparable sport-setting experience (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).
23	
24	**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement can hold a team's progress back (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.
27

14	# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision
15	
16	**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("first clinical review within X hours," "imaging expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). Agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. **Eric's baseline:** "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as a departmental operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. # The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). Note: the workbook's own behaviour-category list (Section A3) shows only three labels — Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst — omitting "Beacon"; whether Beacon is a dropped top tier or a later course revision is not resolved in this corpus.

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose is developmental, not evaluative: leaders use the grid to spot skill gaps and plan continuing professional development, and staff use it to compare self-assessment against supervisor feedback (Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 02:10–04:04). Splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions: a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick mentors with comparable sport-setting experience (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 06:10–07:18) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]].

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Any real personnel decision built on it would still need direct evidence, fair process, and Baylor HR policy (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 07:18–08:02).

**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement can hold a team's progress back (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-mentors-with-sport-specific-experience]] — the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

lines: **What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated** — named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria** — pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options** — progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership** — who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step** — the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("first clinical review within X hours," "imaging expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

-**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). Agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.

# Your Computer Is Probably Your Most Underused Piece of Performance Technology

**What it is** — Weber's claim, made twice in the course (Lab 1C transcript and PDF), that the laptop most practitioners already own outranks any device they might buy next: "it's the most powerful piece of performance tech you own," yet "most people use computers like their typewriter" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:01:13–00:01:29; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). He frames the gap as capability, not access: what a staff member can build, automate, analyze, visualize, and report determines what the rest of the tech stack is worth. His own example, per the transcript (which renders "strength and conditioning" as "straight conditioning," an evident ASR error): "I've been a [strength and] conditioning coach for over 30 years, but I can code fluently, I can run machine learning models, I can build AI tools within my system, I can build websites" (00:01:46–00:02:05).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale ties directly to his data-information-knowledge-wisdom hierarchy (see [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]]): "you can't do that without using your computer and advanced computer skills" (00:02:09–00:02:20). A department can own every wearable and force plate on the market and still be unable to turn the resulting exports into an interpretable report if no one on staff can code or build a dashboard.

**When to apply** — When auditing staff capability alongside equipment (Lab 2B's capability-and-workflow audit; see [[framework--capability-and-workflow-audit-matrix]]), or when deciding where professional-development time should go before the next equipment purchase. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own gap analysis names sport-specific data dictionaries and Baylor-specific technology workflows as unfinished, prioritized work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3]. **Inference:** that work depends on exactly this computer/coding capability existing on staff, not just on the vendor tools themselves.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is careful to say "you don't need to become a programmer" (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1); this is not a claim that every S&C coach must learn to code, only that the department's analytic ceiling is set by whoever's computer skill is highest. It also doesn't specify which skills matter most (spreadsheets vs. dashboards vs. scripting) or how to build them; it names the gap, not the curriculum.

**Example** — Weber's own audit question set for this category: what computer do you actually have, what do you use beyond spreadsheets, and can you run data workflows or dashboards when needed (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this claim is drawn from. [[framework--data-information-knowledge-wisdom-hierarchy]] — why computer skill is the bottleneck between data and decisions.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: he calls it "an old Russian coaching accent" at one point in the transcript (an evident ASR mishearing, likely "concept" or similar) and, later in the same recording, "an old thing. It's not mine." The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Naming the means first also gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: he calls it "an old Russian coaching accent" at one point in the transcript (an evident ASR mishearing, likely "concept" or similar) and, later in the same recording, "an old thing. It's not mine." The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.

# The Capability and Workflow Audit Matrix

**What it is** — A two-part audit that extends Lab 1C's tech-stack inventory (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]) from what a department has to what it produces and who acts on it. The **capability audit** is the "tool truth": what a technology measures, what it does not measure, and where its use shifts from measurement into inference (Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf p.1). The **workflow audit** covers who captures the data, how it is processed (vendor software, in-house code, dashboards), who interprets it, how it is communicated, and where the decision actually gets made (p.1). Built as a matrix: technologies down the rows, applications across the columns (either by domain — rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring — or by question — hamstring injury, speed development, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring). Each cell gets four entries: purpose (what question it answers), output (the metric/report delivered), owner (who is responsible), and workflow (capture to process to interpret to communicate to decision) (pp.1–2).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism: "a device doesn't create impact. A workflow does" (p.1). In small environments alignment happens informally because people talk constantly; as staff, tools, and handoffs multiply, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (p.1). The matrix forces that design decision into a written artifact rather than leaving it as tribal knowledge that breaks when a single staff member leaves. The same audit embeds a delegation model: Weber frames the department's direction and standards as "the highway" and staff's day-to-day tool and timing choices as "changing lanes," with the matrix giving staff **tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment** (p.1–2); see [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] for the fuller treatment of that mental model.

**When to apply** — Onboarding new staff, identifying budget or technology gaps, or auditing an existing department for handoff risk. **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and Athletic Medicine's decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a stated final-decision role [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play], and Eric's own gap analysis names the department's reporting model as currently under-specified [method-baseline.md, Department model]. **Inference:** Weber's worked example (hamstring rehab triangulation: force transducer for strength trend, GPS/IMU for exposure dose, mechanics check for strategy change, response checks at 24 hours) is structurally identical to that shared workflow, and this matrix is a concrete way to specify exactly which discipline owns each step of it.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a documentation and role-clarity exercise, not a validation of any individual test's reliability (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] and [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question). Weber's own hamstring/deceleration examples are illustrations of matrix structure, not a validated injury-assessment or programming pathway.

**Example** — Weber's deceleration-capacity workflow: GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events, data is processed (Python/R/SpeedSig), the output becomes a trend report plus exposure-tolerance summary, and the decision becomes a programming adjustment to load, density, or drill selection (p.3).

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the prior-step audit this one builds on. [[framework--strategy-as-highway-tactics-as-lanes]] — the delegation model embedded in this matrix. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — where the "decision" cell of this matrix gets formalized.

# A Rolling Baseline Can Hide the Exact Long-Term Drift You Are Trying to Catch

**What it is** — Weber's specific caution inside the monitoring-vs-testing framework (see [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]): rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are excellent at answering "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week," but they are not designed to answer "did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase" — because the reference point (the rolling average itself) moves along with the slow change you would need to detect (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1–2). His fix: long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs. post, block vs. block), not continuous smoothing (p.2).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** a rolling window is, by construction, always chasing the most recent values. If an athlete's true capacity drifts down gradually over eight weeks, a rolling average would likely track that drift and never flag it as a deviation, because the reference point itself has quietly moved with the athlete. The same window that makes short-term monitoring useful (fast reaction to recent change) is what makes it blind to slow change. Weber himself states the effect (rolling averages answer a different question than phase-level testing) without spelling out this mechanism.

**When to apply** — Any metric tracked with a rolling window or EWMA for daily/weekly monitoring that is also, informally or formally, being used to answer a phase-level question of whether the athlete's capacity actually improved. **Eric's baseline:** weekly tracking is stated as preferred over infrequent, once-a-phase testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this heuristic is the specific mechanism behind the broader tension flagged in [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] between Weber's framework and that stated preference.

**When NOT to apply** — This is not an argument against rolling averages for their intended purpose (short-term status and load-adjustment decisions); it is a warning against also treating the same rolling number as evidence of long-term program effectiveness. It also does not specify how wide a rolling window should be for a given metric, only that no window substitutes for a genuine pre/post or block/block comparison.

**Example** — Weber's own instruction: to evaluate a training phase, compare defined phases or time points (pre-season start vs. end, block one vs. block two) rather than relying on the continuous smoothing used for weekly monitoring (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.1).

**Related** — [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the parent framework this heuristic sits inside. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — the statistics for deciding whether any observed change, rolling or block-based, is real.

# The Kaigi Decision Meeting

**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow (Kaigi-transcript summary, 00:00–02:18). **Inference:** forcing preparation and concise contributions likely works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.

**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone — aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Kaigi-transcript summary, 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that a decision meeting has different requirements from sharing information, creating solutions, or educating staff (00:00–02:18); using kaigi structure to force a decision before the options are actually narrowed to two or three, or before enough evidence exists, will produce a fast but poorly grounded call. His own Go/No-Go numbers (roughly 15–17 staff, under 30 seconds per player, 20-minute follow-up) are his example's parameters, not validated operating thresholds or a recommended clinical protocol. See [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for the broader set of meeting modes; kaigi is specifically the **decide** mode and should not be reached for when the actual need is **diagnose** or **build**.

**Example** — Weber's stalled-meeting rescue: when a broader problem-solving discussion stalls, explicitly announce the switch to decision mode, give it a fixed short window (his example: 10 minutes), and require a stated decision, an owner, and a documented outcome before the group moves on (12:14–13:23).

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the record-keeping this format requires. [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] — the broader typology this format sits inside. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — the companion presentation format for the evidence brought into a kaigi-style meeting.

# Stoplight Storytelling

**What it is** — A short, repeatable presentation format for bringing a decision to a group: state the question or headline first (rather than opening with data that has no stated purpose); show status using green (go), amber (hold/monitor), or red (stop/change); present at most one chart, readable immediately, that addresses whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence; and close with a requested direction (start/stop/change) plus one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 00:00–04:25; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Presentation rules: keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, avoid dual axes and complex charts that require extended explanation, never bring multiple charts, multiple requests, or brand-new information into the moment, and give every status, including amber, a next action or review date (04:25–06:23). A roughly two-minute presentation is Weber's own benchmark, though he notes novel or complex issues may need pre-reading or a separate meeting instead (06:23–06:43).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to keep a sequence of presentations in one meeting from expanding into long, unfocused discussions, and to let staff present more autonomously once the shared format is understood (06:56–07:54). **Inference:** forcing one chart and one request likely removes the two most common ways a presentation drifts, adding more evidence than the room can process in the time available, and leaving the ask implicit so no decision actually gets made.

**When to apply** — Any recurring review where multiple practitioners each need to bring a status update that may require a decision: a weekly return-to-play review, a load-monitoring standup, or a technology-adoption check-in. Pairs directly with the kaigi format's evidence-precision rule (see [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]) as the visual layer of the same discipline.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber's two-minute benchmark and single-chart rule are explicitly not meant for novel or complex issues, which he says may need pre-reading or a dedicated meeting instead (06:23–06:43); forcing a genuinely complex, multi-variable problem into stoplight format risks the same false simplicity the framework is designed to avoid elsewhere (see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]). The timing and efficiency claims are Weber's own practice examples, not validated thresholds.

**Example** — Weber's practical template, stated directly: question, then green/amber/red status, then one clear chart with uncertainty and supporting context, then requested direction, then owner/due date/review (07:54 close, restated as the lab's summary template).

**Related** — [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]] — the closing record this format requires. [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — the meeting format this presentation style is built to feed. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the caution against over-simplifying a genuinely complex decision.

# Judge a Technology by Its Adoption Stage, Not Just Its Existence

**What it is** — Weber applies Rogers' innovation-adoption curve to performance technology: a tool's usefulness to a given department depends on where it sits on the maturity curve (early/skeptical adopters through mainstream use), not just on whether it exists or is popular elsewhere. His example: GPS moved from being met with skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35).

**Why it works** — Weber does not state a mechanism for this framework beyond the GPS example itself. **Inference:** adopting a technology before an environment's procedures, staff skill, and interpretive norms have matured to match it likely recreates the tech-rich/procedure-poor problem he names in Lab 1C (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]): the tool exists, but the surrounding discipline needed to use it well does not yet exist.

**When to apply** — Weighing a genuinely new technology (a novel wearable, an AI-based analysis tool) against an established one with known error, interpretation norms, and staff familiarity. The question this framework poses is not whether the tool is valid in principle, but whether the tool, and the staff's ability to use it, have matured to the point where adopting it now is worth the transition cost.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber gives no criteria for placing a specific tool on the curve, and the maturity claim here is his own retrospective narrative about GPS, not a measured or validated adoption metric for any other technology. It should not be read as an argument to always wait for mainstream adoption; earlier-stage tools can still be worth adopting deliberately, with the added discipline that comes with being an early user.

**Example** — Weber's GPS timeline, per the lesson summary: he contrasts early adopters of new tools with GPS specifically, which he says moved from skepticism in a 1998 meeting to routine professional use (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 04:30–07:35). This is his personal recollection, not a documented industry history in this corpus.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that reveals whether a department's procedures have caught up to a tool it already owns.

# Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** this is itself a live example of the kind of undocumented drift this principle warns against.

**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run; a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). It also does not by itself tell you the size of the error band a given procedure produces — that requires the reliability statistics in [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]].

**Example** — Weber places any single product or test within a wider system: he warns against treating one red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete, and against collecting a measure without a defined question behind it (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24, 08:45–09:19) — both symptoms of a department that has not documented what a given result is supposed to trigger.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit that catches undocumented procedure. # Protocol Drift: A Test Can Keep Its Name While Everything Else Changes

**What it is** — Weber's term for a specific reliability failure mode: a test keeps the same name over time while its warm-up, positioning, verbal instructions, or acceptance rules quietly change, so results are no longer comparable across sessions or staff even though the label on the report looks consistent (Podcast 1 summary, 02:19–03:03 and 04:24–05:31). His fix is the same one from Lab 1C: standardize and document those details before comparing results across time or personnel (see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]]).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** protocol drift is dangerous specifically because it is likely invisible in the data itself; a change in average or peak value looks like an athlete change unless someone knows the procedure changed underneath it. Weber's own stated companion point, per the lesson summary, is a statistical-interpretation one: know the tool's and the local process's reliability before calling any individual change meaningful, and distinguish measurement noise from a change that warrants action (Podcast 1 summary, 03:03–03:17, 05:31–06:48).

# The Decision Log: Action, Owner, Due Date, Review

**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format, per the lesson summaries: the meeting-typology **decide** mode requires an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale, per the lesson summary, is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed (Kaigi-transcript summary, 04:48–05:56). **Inference:** without a record, a verbal decision is likely subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). **Eric's baseline:** no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus, even though KPI-threshold identification is named as a departmental operating principle [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** a decision log does not supply the missing criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale — Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

**Example** — Weber's stoplight-storytelling version adds one more requirement to the same four fields, per the lesson summary: every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date (Lab 3C summary, 05:51–06:23), closing the loophole of an ambiguous "wait and see" outcome with no owner attached.

**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]] — where this log format originates in the course. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — the more detailed version of "next step" for higher-stakes decisions. [[framework--stoplight-storytelling-format]] — the presentation format that ends with this same log.

# Data to Information to Knowledge to Wisdom

**What it is** — Weber uses the standard data-information-knowledge-wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy to argue that storing measurements and building dashboards (data, information) does not, by itself, help a department make a decision (knowledge, wisdom); each step up the hierarchy requires additional interpretive work, not just more collection (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 03:27–04:42).

**Why it works** — Weber's stated mechanism connects directly to communication capacity: a coach or medical colleague handed a complex dashboard is left to do the interpretation themselves, which the lesson summary describes with a pick-up-52 analogy — see [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the recipient is handed a scattered deck and asked to reassemble it into an answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 04:42–07:44).

**When to apply** — Reviewing any recurring report or dashboard against the question of whether it hands the reader raw data or hands them an answer they can act on. **Eric's baseline:** the Playbook's Development Plan already names "standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates" as unfinished Phase 2 work [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]. **Inference:** this hierarchy is a way to test a draft template before it ships (does it stop at data, or does it reach a stated recommendation).

**When NOT to apply** — The DIKW hierarchy is a widely used general communication model, not something original to Weber or specific to sport performance; he offers no sport-science-specific validation of it, only an application. It also does not specify how to move from one level to the next for a particular metric, only that the movement is necessary.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring caution: treating one favorable test result as a complete return-to-running answer is data or information, not knowledge, because it has not been checked against other convergent evidence (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); see [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] for the fuller version of this same caution.

**Related** — [[heuristic--lead-with-the-recipients-question-not-the-dashboard]] — the communication practice this hierarchy motivates. [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — the evidentiary discipline needed to reach "knowledge." [[heuristic--computer-is-your-most-underused-tool]] — the practical bottleneck Weber ties to moving up this hierarchy.

# Discipline Equals Freedom: Procedure, Not the Device, Creates Trust

**What it is** — Weber's closing chain in Lab 1C, credited to Jocko Willink's "discipline equals freedom": **discipline gives you reliability, reliability gives you confidence, confidence gives you decisions you can defend** (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4; Lab 1C transcript 00:05:35–00:05:54). The claim just before it: "reliability doesn't live in the device. It's in your procedures. A procedure is fundamentally a hidden multiplier" (transcript 00:04:45–00:05:02). Weber returns to the same chain twice more in the course. In Webinar 3 he operationalizes it as three practices — document repeatable procedures, set strategic direction with explicit decision boundaries, and give staff regular direct feedback — on the stated argument that this reduces ambiguity and gives both leaders and staff more room for focused work (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–00:38). In Module 6B Part B he applies the same chain to interdisciplinary communication: "the better educated the staff are... the less translation is needed. That frees up time for decision-making, problem-solving, and adaptation in real time" (Module_6B_Part_B PDF p.1).

**Why it works** — Weber's mechanism is that undocumented procedures create ambiguity, and ambiguity is what forces re-explanation, second-guessing, and disputes after the fact ("we took two measurements... which one is right?" PDF p.4). Writing the procedure down once removes the need to re-litigate it under pressure, which is what frees attention for harder problems.

**When to apply** — Any point where Eric is deciding whether a documented SOP is worth the paperwork: onboarding a new staff member or intern, standardizing a force-plate or GPS procedure, or writing a credential-vault protocol. **Eric's baseline:** a secure credential-vault protocol is already named as needed but not yet implemented [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4], and the intern curriculum's stated design principle is to teach "the how" (hands-on technical training) alongside "the why" (conceptual education) [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1]. **Inference:** the how is the procedure that makes the why defensible later.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a claim about where trust in a decision comes from, not a claim that more documentation is always better; Weber gives no guidance on how much procedure is enough or when documentation itself becomes the bottleneck. It also assumes the underlying test or measure is worth running at all — see [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] for that prior question.

**Example** — Weber's own test: "if you started a job this week as a lead in a department, would you be able to walk in and say, this is how we're going to operate?" (Lab 1C transcript, 00:05:13–00:05:23). **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's own Playbook still documents a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord collection SOP, even though roster-wide NordBord testing for football was retired after January 2023 [method-baseline.md Tensions #8]. **Inference:** this is the failure mode Weber warns against here, a procedure that fell out of sync with a decision that had already been made.

**Related** — [[framework--tech-stack-inventory-by-measurement-system]] — the audit this principle closes out. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]] — a structure that depends on this same procedure-first discipline. [[heuristic--set-communication-channel-and-timing-rules]] — the communication-specific application from Webinar 3.

In Part III he adds three more standing practices from the same "discipline equals freedom" chain (see [[principle--discipline-equals-freedom]]): document routine work so it is clear who handles equipment, session prep, data collection, and testing; remove avoidable ambiguity by stating a meeting's purpose, deadline, and each person's role; and schedule regular feedback check-ins, addressing performance issues promptly and asking staff for feedback on the leader's own leadership (Webinar 3 Part III summary, 00:00–09:15).

# Measurement vs. Inference

**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples: calling a lower countermovement-jump result "neurological fatigue," or a GPS change "tissue stress" — neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

**Why it works** — **Inference:** collapsing the distinction likely lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02) — the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] — combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] — whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]] — the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

# Decide the Means Before the Modality, and the Modality Before the Technology

**What it is** — Weber's ordering rule for any training, testing, or monitoring decision: first name the **means** (the physical quality or question you are trying to change or answer, e.g. "improve reactive strength" or "assess hamstring capacity"), then choose the **modality** (the drill, test, or method), and only then pick the **technology**. Weber twice credits means-versus-modality to someone else, not himself: he calls it "an old Russian coaching accent" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:53–00:02:00; an evident ASR mishearing, likely "concept" or similar) and, later in the same recording, "an old thing. It's not mine" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:09:37–00:09:41). The same modality can serve different means: a sprint dribble drill can teach frontside mechanics or teach vertical force application depending on the coach's intent (Lab 1A transcript, 00:01:28–00:03:09). He restates the same ordering twice more across the course: in Webinar 1 Part II, the summary reports that staff should begin with the athlete question or problem and only then select a measurement tool, rather than starting from the equipment on hand (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 00:00–02:14); and in Lab 2C's written material, the operating principle is stated directly: "Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then choose the technology" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2).

**Why it works** — Weber's rationale: when technology leads, "we have force plates, so we should jump" and "we have GPS, so we should report something" become the operating logic, which he calls technology-led practice that "creates noise" (Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf p.2). Weber's own stated point is that without this shared language, "if people don't get that context, they're going to struggle with your communication" (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:52–00:03:57). **Inference:** naming the means first likely gives staff a shared reason for a drill or test, so a leader can ask "what's the mean, why are you doing it?" and get an answer staff and athletes can act on (Lab 1A transcript, 00:03:42–00:04:32).

**When to apply** — Any time a new device, test, or drill is proposed because it is available rather than because a specific quality or question has been named first. **Eric's baseline:** Baylor's current Applied Performance data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport or question, which Eric's own gap analysis already flags as a usability problem [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]. **Inference:** this principle gives that gap a specific fix order, name the question and quality per sport first, then map which existing technology already answers it, before adding anything new.

**When NOT to apply** — Weber is explicit that the technology still has real limitations that shape what's possible ("the technology is going to have limitations, of course, but the technology may be able to be applied in different ways," Lab 1A transcript, 00:04:38–00:04:50); this is an ordering rule for decision-making, not a claim that tool constraints are irrelevant. It also does not resolve which quality matters most for a given sport or phase, only the sequence in which the question gets asked.

**Example** — Weber's CM2 athlete-stage map (see [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]]) is the means-first vocabulary he built to make this ordering usable day to day: staff say where an athlete sits (control, movement, capacity, maximum) before discussing which drill or device to use next.

**Related** — [[framework--cm2-athlete-progression-map]] — the shared-language framework this principle is meant to produce. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] — the same purpose-first ordering applied specifically to monitoring vs. testing decisions. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — the companion discipline once a measurement is in hand.
